en: When the night of Brahmā had passed and the Lotus-born One had awakened, Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged by the waters.
Just as in former ages he took delight in sporting in the water, he assumed the auspicious form of a boar and raised up the earth from the cosmic eggs.
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts his tusks, the rituals his teeth, and the fire-altars his mouth;
Agni is his tongue, the darbha grass his hair, and the Veda his head—such is he of great ascetic power.
The divine one has day and night for his eyes, the Vedāṅgas and the Śruti for his ornaments,
clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his beak, and the sound of the Sāmaveda for his great voice.
Consisting of the truth of the Dharma, glorious, honored by his successive strides,
with a great snout for expiation, knees like those of a beast, and of massive form.
The Udgātṛ priest is his intestines; the sacrificial oblation is his characteristic mark; the seeds and medicinal herbs are his great fruit;
the altar is his inner self; the mantras are his buttocks; and the Soma juice is his blood.
The altar was his shoulder, the sacrificial oblation his fragrance; he possessed the momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the *prāgvaṃśa* hall was his body, radiant and endowed with various initiations (*dīkṣā*).
The Great Yoga has the Dakṣiṇā as its heart, consists of the Great Mantra, and is beautiful with the Upākarma as its lips; it is adorned with the whirlpools of the Pravargya rite.
His path of movement through various meters, seated upon the secret Upanishads,
accompanied by his consort Chāyā, he indeed rose up like the peak of a jewel-mountain.

The Lord, the primordial god and great yogi, having entered the single ocean, lifted up with the tip of his tusk the earth— bounded by the oceans and including its mountains, groves, and forests— which had been submerged in the waters of that single ocean; desiring the welfare of the worlds, he fashioned the world anew.
Thus, in ancient times, having assumed the form of the Sacrificial Boar and desiring the welfare of all beings, the divine Earth was raised up from the depths of the netherworld.

Having extracted them and established them in their own respective stable locations, Madhusūdana divided the waters according to their proper places: the oceanic waters into the oceans and the riverine waters into the rivers. He likewise fashioned the seven netherworlds (pātālas), the seven worlds (lokas), and the various locations for the continents and the seas.
The guardians of the quarters, the world-protectors, the rivers, the mountains and forest trees, the seven seers who know the Dharma, the Vedas with their auxiliary branches, and the gods and asuras.
Piśācas, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans; cattle, birds, wild animals, and the fourfold assembly of beings; as well as clouds, rainbows, lightning, and various sacrifices.
Thus the Blessed One Varāha, having created this world with all its moving and unmoving beings, departed for that destination of the worlds which is unknown.
When Janārdana, the god of gods, had departed for an unknown destination, the Earth reflected: "What support will there be for me?"
"I shall go and ask Kaśyapa; he will tell me without a doubt, for that great sage is constantly occupied with my concerns."
Having thus made her resolve, the goddess, assuming the form of a woman, went to see Kaśyapa, and Kaśyapa beheld her.

Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her face resembled the autumnal moon, her hair was adorned with swarms of bees, and she was radiant and auspicious, with lips as red as the bandhujīva flower.
She had beautiful eyebrows, very fine teeth, a lovely nose, and arched brows;
she possessed a neck like a conch shell, joined thighs, and full, rounded hips and thighs.
Her two breasts shone, being symmetrical, full, and close together;
her arms were as tender as lotus stalks, and her hands resembled young sprouts;
her thighs were like pillars of gold, and her knees were hidden and joined.
Her shanks were hairless and perfectly symmetrical, her feet exceedingly beautiful,
and her hips and waist were firm like those of a lion cub.
Her copper-colored nails were endowed with radiance, her form was captivating to all,
and she constantly made the quarters of the sky appear filled with blue lotuses by means of her glances.
The goddess, making the quarters free from darkness with her radiance,
was clad in very fine white garments and adorned with the finest jewels.
Making the earth appear as if covered with lotuses by her footsteps,
she was endowed with beauty and youth, yet stood before him with humble demeanor.
Seeing her approach and having honored her, Kaśyapa said to her, "O lady of beautiful hips, that which was in your heart has been understood by me."
"O large-eyed one, bear this in mind; go, O Goddess, to Janārdana.
He will explain to you in its entirety how your future steadfastness shall be."
O lady of auspicious countenance, O lovely-limbed one, I have learned through the power of meditative yoga—by his grace—that his dwelling is in the Ocean of Milk, all for your sake.
Having been addressed in this manner, the Earth then honored Kaśyapa and departed for the Ocean of Milk, the sea, in order to see Keśava.
She beheld that treasury of nectar, enchanting as the rays of the moon, agitated by hundreds of waves produced by the turbulence of the wind.
Resembling a hundred Himalayas, it was like another orb of the earth,
appearing as if it were calling out to the ground with its moving hands of waves.
By those very [rays], as if incessantly bestowing whiteness upon the moon,
he was rendered free from every stain by Hari dwelling within him.
Therefore, he who maintains a very white and powerful body— pale, moving through the air, and dwelling in the subterranean realm— is invincible.
Rich with sapphire-like dark-red blossoms, it was like the sky turned upside down, or like a forest grove covered by the emergence of clusters of fruit.
Having seen him standing there in the midst, he beheld the abode of Keśava.
Upon that [couch], he beheld Madhusūdana reclining on his side, his dimensions indescribable and endowed with inconceivable supernatural power.
His lotus-face was difficult to discern due to the rays from the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa;
it resembled a hundred moons and possessed a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
Akṣobhya, clad in yellow garments and adorned with all kinds of jewels,
shines resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and with two earrings.
His pair of feet were being massaged by the auspicious palms of Lakṣmī,
while he was being attended on all sides by personified weapons.
Seeing that lotus-eyed Madhusūdana, she paid homage to him:
"O God, I, who had gone to the depths of the netherworld (rasātala), have been uplifted by you; O Viṣṇu, I have been established in my own place out of your desire for the welfare of the worlds."
"In this matter, O Lord of Gods, what consolation will there now be for me? When she had spoken thus, the God addressed these words to the Goddess:
O Earth, the virtuous who delight in the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life, and who are solely devoted to the scriptures, will support you; upon them your burden has been placed.
Thus addressed, Vasumatī spoke to the God of gods: "O Eternal One, declare the duties of the social classes and the stages of life."
I wish to hear from you, for you are my supreme refuge;
salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the strength of the enemies of the gods!
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace;
O Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, you of great strength and prowess!
O Lord beyond the senses, O You who are so difficult to cross over, O Wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
O Boar, O Terrible One, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person!
O golden-haired one, O all-seeing one, O embodiment of sacrifice, O stainless one;
O Lord of the field and the knower of the field, O Lord of gods, O you who recline upon the ocean of waters!
O you who are the agent of the creation and destruction of this entire world!
O Knower of Dharma and Adharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons,
O Teacher of the seven-headed sacrifice, O Supreme Ancient Being!
O Lord of the eternal syllable, most subtle Master, compassionate toward devotees, and purifier;
you are the refuge of all the gods, and you are the refuge of those who discourse on Brahman.
O Supreme Person, you are the goal of those who have known what is to be known; O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Lord of the Speech-Master.
To Subrahmaṇya, the invincible, the son of Vasuṣeṇa who bestows wealth,
endowed with the power of great yoga, the one born from Pṛśni, who maintains the radiant flame.
To the high-souled Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed, the infallible,
the god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, the all-pervading Lord, the great sovereign of all beings.

"O Blessed One, tell me of the single manifestation, the four-armed one, the cause of the causes of the world; and tell me of the eternal dharmas for the four castes, joined with the conduct of the stages of life (āśrama), together with their secrets and their summaries.
Thus addressed by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth:
Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes, together with the conduct of the stages of life, including their secret doctrines and essential summaries.
O lady of beautiful thighs, sit upon this excellent golden seat as the ultimate refuge for those virtuous ones who shall uphold you.
Then, while seated comfortably upon the earth, she heard the Vaiṣṇava duties.
Oṃ! The four castes are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among them, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the entire collection of rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with the funeral rite is performed according to the mantras.
And their phenomena [are also included].
Teaching for a Brāhmaṇa.
For a Kṣatriya, there is constant devotion to weapons.
For a Vaiśya, the protection of cattle.
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born.
For the twice-born, [the duties are] sacrificing and studying.
Now, their functions are as follows.
For a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and receiving gifts [are lawful means of livelihood].
The protection of the earth is the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and the breeding of livestock are the duties of a Vaiśya.
For the Śūdra, all crafts.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, generosity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion.
Straightforwardness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins, and likewise absence of malice—this is called the common dharma.
Now follow the duties of kings.
The protection of the subjects.
The establishment of the social classes and stages of life in their respective duties.
And the king should take refuge in a region that is arid yet suitable for cattle and endowed with crops.
And it consists mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
In that regard, one should take refuge in one of the following types of fortresses: those protected by deserts, large tracts of land, water, trees, or mountains.
And remaining there, he should appoint the local chiefs over their respective villages.
The ten superintendents.
The supervisors of a hundred.
And [he should appoint] provincial governors.
The village headman shall provide a remedy for the faults of the village.
If he is unable [to do so], he should report it to the superintendent of ten villages.
He too, being unable [to do so], [reports it] to the superintendent of a hundred.
He, too, being unable [to do it himself], [should entrust it] to the provincial governor.
The governor of the region, too, should eradicate wrongdoing with his whole being.
He should appoint trustworthy persons to oversee mines, tolls, ferries, and elephant forests.
Those who are most righteous in matters of dharma.
Skilled in matters of purposeful action.
The brave ones in the acts of battle.
Eunuchs among women.
For the purpose of tribute from the subjects, he shall take a sixth part of the grain every year.
And from all the crops.
Two hundred [paṇas] shall be paid for cattle, gold, and garments.
From meat, honey, ghee, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, fruits, juices, wood, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and wickerwork, the king shall take a sixth part.
One should not collect taxes from Brahmins.
For they are the ones who bring about the king's righteousness.
And the king receives a sixth part of the merits and demerits of his subjects.
And from goods produced in his own country, he shall take a tenth part as customs duty.
And from foreign merchandise, a twentieth part [shall be taken].
If he departs from the customs station, he shall incur the forfeiture of his entire property.

Artisans and those who live by manual labor shall perform work for the king for one month each year. The constituent elements of the state are the sovereign, the minister, the fort, the treasury, the army, the territory, and the ally.
And he should put to death those who defile it.
And he should have the eyes of spies regarding both his own kingdom and the kingdoms of others.
One should perform the worship of the virtuous.
And he should slay those who are wicked.
One should employ conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force against enemies, friends, neutrals, and those in the middle position as appropriate and at the proper time.
And he should resort, as the occasion demands, to peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, or the double stratagem.
One should set out on the journey in either the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa.
Or when another is in distress.
Upon arriving in a foreign land, one should not abandon the customs of that country.
And when attacked by an enemy, he should protect his own kingdom with his whole soul.
For kings, there is no duty equal to the sacrifice of one's body in battle.
Those who are killed while protecting cows, Brahmins, kings, friends, wealth, wives, or their own lives, partake of the heavenly world.
And for the sake of protecting against the intermixture of castes.
Upon the conquest of another's city, the king should install one born of that family there as the ruler.
One should not destroy a royal family.
Except for a royal family of ignoble birth.
One should avoid indulgence in hunting, gambling, women, and drinking.
And [the same applies] to verbal abuse and physical assault.
One should not commit a corruption of the meaning.
One should not cut off the primary gateways.
One should not shower [gifts] upon an unworthy recipient.
One should take everything from the mines.
Having found a treasure, one should give half of it to the Brahmins.
One should cause the second half to enter the treasury.
A Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure-trove, may take it all.
A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king, a fourth part to the Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself.
A Vaiśya, however, should give a fourth part to the king, half to the Brāhmaṇas, and take a fourth part for himself.
And a Śūdra, having divided what he has acquired into twelve parts, shall give five shares to the king, five shares to the Brāhmaṇas, and take two shares for himself.
One should confiscate everything from one who has not reported what he knows.
Except for Brāhmaṇas, they shall give a twelfth part of what was deposited by themselves to the king.
One who claims that what was deposited by another was deposited by oneself shall incur a fine equal to the value of that property.
The king shall protect the property of minors, of those without a protector, and of women.
Having recovered wealth stolen by thieves, he shall give it all back to those of every social class from whom it was taken.
And if he cannot obtain it from his own treasury, he should give it from [the treasury] itself.
One should pacify the afflictions caused by fate through the means of propitiatory rites and auspicious ceremonies.
And there will be destructions by foreign armies due to the constant prevalence of weapons.
One should choose as a domestic priest (purohita) a man of noble birth, free from physical defects, ascetic, and skilled in the meaning of the Vedas, Itihāsas, and Dharmaśāstras.
[He should appoint] those who are pure, free from greed, attentive, endowed with capability, and capable of assisting in all matters.
He himself should preside over legal proceedings together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
In the administration of justice, he should appoint either a Brāhmaṇa.

The king should appoint as members of his council those who possess noble birth, proper conduct, and the observance of vows; who are impartial toward both enemy and friend; and who cannot be subverted by desire, anger, fear, greed, or other motives for personal gain.
And the king shall be dependent upon the astrologer in all matters.
One should constantly worship the gods and the brahmins.
One should be a servant of the elders.
And one who performs sacrifices.
And within his realm, no Brahmin shall perish from the pangs of hunger.
Nor is there anyone else devoted to virtuous deeds.
And one should bestow land upon the Brāhmaṇas.

And to those to whom he should grant it—his own kinsmen—he should give a document written on cloth or a copper plate, recording the extent of the land and a description of the boundaries of the gift, and marked with his own seal, for the information of future kings.
And one should not seize land given by another.
One should always bestow all gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas.
But one should protect oneself from all sides.
And it should be beautiful to behold.
And he is one who holds the mantras for antidotes that destroy poison.
One should not employ anything that has not been examined.
One should speak with a smile as a preliminary.
One should not even frown at those who deserve to be executed.
And he should cause punishment to be inflicted upon those deserving of it in accordance with their offense.
He should administer punishment correctly.
He would not forgive anyone for a second offense.
For kings, there is no one who does not deserve punishment for failing to protect their own duty.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks fearlessly, there the subjects prosper, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
He should maintain just punishment within his own kingdom, severe punishment toward enemies, straightforwardness toward friends, and be endowed with forgiveness toward affectionate Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain, his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
The king who is happy in the happiness of his subjects and who is pained by their suffering is endowed with fame in this world and is glorified in heaven after death.
The dust particle situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [transitional particles] make one *likṣā*.
Six of those [yūkās] make one barleycorn (yava).
Three of those [rattis] constitute one *kṛṣṇala*.
Five of those [rathacakras] make one māṣa.
Twelve of those [finger-breadths] constitute half an *akṣa*.
Half an akṣa, together with four māṣakas, is one suvarṇa.
A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*.
Two *kṛṣṇala*s weighed together constitute one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those constitute a dharaṇa.
A copper *kārṣika* is a *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are recorded as the first *sāhasa* fine; five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand is the highest.
Now, all those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin), with the exception of Brāhmaṇas, are to be put to death.
A Brāhmaṇa shall not be subjected to corporal punishment.
He shall banish from his own country a Brāhmaṇa who has been branded with a mark.
And for that [offense], one should fashion a headless human figure upon his forehead to represent the murder of a Brahmin.
A tavern sign [is the mark] for the consumption of liquor.
For theft, the punishment is the branding with the mark of a dog's foot.
The female organ [is the limb] for approaching the bed of one's guru.
In other cases of capital offenses as well, he should banish one who possesses full wealth and remains unhurt.
And the king shall put to death those who forge royal edicts.
And those who forge documents.
Poisoners, arsonists, irresistible thieves, and those who kill women, children, or men.
And those who would steal more than ten jars of grain.
More than one hundred [measures] of those things that are measured by weight.
And those who are of low birth who might desire the kingdom.
And those who destroy bridges.
And those who forcibly provide shelter and food to thieves.
Except in cases of the king's incapacity.
A woman whose husband is incapable [of providing for her] and one who has transgressed [her duty].
If a person of inferior caste commits an offense against one of superior caste with a particular limb, that very limb shall be cut off from him.
One who sits on a single seat with a mark made upon his hip shall be banished; one who spits shall be deprived of both lips.
And he is unable to pass wind and is devoid of an anus.
And one who reviles has a forked tongue.
The king shall pour boiling oil into the mouth of those who, out of arrogance, provide instruction on the Dharma.
And if one mentions another's name or caste with malice, a ten-finger-long wooden stake shall be driven into his body.
One who speaks falsely regarding learning, country, caste, or occupation shall be fined two hundred kārśāpaṇas.
Even one who speaks the truth regarding those who are one-eyed, lame, and so forth, shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas.
One who insults his teachers shall pay two hundred kārśāpaṇas.
But when an accusation of an offense involving loss of caste is made against another, the highest amercement shall be imposed.
For one who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka), the middle [fine] applies.
In the case of insulting those advanced in the three Vedas and in assemblies of caste-groups.
And for [theft from] a village or a district, the first amercement shall be imposed.
In the case of an insult involving a physical deformity, the fine shall be one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
For insulting someone of equal caste, one shall be fined twelve paṇas.
There are six [offenses] for reviling one of inferior appearance or caste.
If one insults another of a superior caste at the appropriate time, the punishment shall be equal to that [of the offense].
Or three kārṣāpaṇas.
But one who violates another's wife shall be punished with the highest amercement if she belongs to his own caste.
In approaching a woman of inferior caste, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
And in sexual intercourse.
One who approaches a woman of the lowest caste deserves death.
For sexual intercourse with a female animal, one shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
And he who gives away a maiden without disclosing her defects.
And he should support her.
One who declares an innocent woman to be guilty shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, or a cow shall be made one-handed and one-footed.
And one who sells meat.
One who slaughters domestic animals shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
He shall pay its value to the owner of the animal.
One who kills a wild animal shall pay fifty kārṣāpaṇas.
A bird-killer and a fisherman shall each pay ten kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who destroys insects shall pay a kārṣāpaṇa.
But one who cuts down a tree that bears fruit commits the highest amercement.
One who cuts down trees that bear flowers or fruit incurs the middle [offense].
One who cuts down creepers, shrubs, or climbing plants shall pay a fine of one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
One [is the offense of] cutting grass.
And all [the people] informed their respective masters of its occurrence.
He will quickly cause ten kārṣāpaṇas to be paid out.
Twenty with the foot.
If with wood, the first amercement.
With a stone, the middling [offering].
With a weapon, [one attains] the highest.
For pulling at the feet, hair, garments, or hands, the fine shall be ten paṇas.
One who causes pain without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas.
Together with blood, sixty-four [thousand].
In the case of breaking a hand, foot, or tooth, or cutting off an ear or nose, the middle [amercement] shall be imposed.
In the obstruction of movement, food, and speech, as well as in the inflicting of blows.
And for the breaking of the eyes, neck, arms, thighs, or shoulders, the highest [amercement] applies.
The king shall not release from bondage for as long as he lives one who pierces both eyes.
Or one should make it exactly like that.
When one person kills many, the punishment for each victim shall be double that which was prescribed for a single case.
Of those standing near him who were crying out but did not run toward him, and of those wandering about.
And all those who cause injury to persons shall pay the expenses incurred for their recovery.
And those who cause suffering to domestic animals.
One who steals a cow, a horse, a camel, or an elephant should be made one-eyed and one-footed.
He is one who does not steal goats or sheep, and he is single-handed.
One who steals grain shall be fined eleven times its value.
And one who steals grain.
One who steals more than fifty measures of gold, silver, or clothing commits the offense of *vikara*.
He who steals less than that shall be fined eleven times the value.

One who steals thread, cotton, cow-dung, molasses, curd, milk, buttermilk, grass, salt, clay, ashes, birds, fish, ghee, oil, meat, honey, articles made of split bamboo, bamboo, earthenware, or metal vessels, as well as cooked food, shall pay three times their value.
For the theft of flowers, green shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or leaves, the fine is five kṛṣṇalas.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One who steals gems shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who steals articles not previously mentioned shall pay a fine equal to their value.
Thieves shall be made to restore everything they have stolen to the owner.
Then, the application of the prescribed punishment was carried out against them.
He who gives a wrong path to those for whom a path must be given shall be fined twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
And he offered a seat to him who was worthy of a seat.
And they failed to honor those worthy of honor.
And also in the case of neglecting an invitation to a neighboring Brāhmaṇa.
And having invited those who would take food.
Having been invited, they said, "So be it," and ate without consuming even a single gold māṣaka.
And for one who provides a dwelling, double the amount of food.
One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall pay a fine of sixteen suvarṇas.
One hundred [times] for one who causes loss of caste.
One who drinks liquor is to be put to death.
For defaming a Kṣatriya, half of that [fine].
To defame a Vaiśya, even half of that [fine] shall be imposed.
For one who defames a Śūdra, the first amercement is prescribed.
One who touches a member of the three higher castes who is not to be touched, by acting out of desire, deserves death.
One should strike a menstruating woman with whips.
One who commits an act of impurity even near a public road, a garden, or water shall be fined one hundred paṇas.
And one should abandon that as well.
One who breaks the ground, walls, or other parts of a house shall be fined the middle amercement.
And one should apply that.
One who throws an injurious substance into another's house shall pay a fine of one hundred paṇas.
And one who denies what is common property.
And one who does not give what has been sent.
And the abandonment of one another by father, son, teacher, patron, and officiating priest, provided they have not fallen from their status.
And one should not abandon them.
And those who feed Śūdras and renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors.
And one who performs unsuitable actions.
And one who breaks into a house by the sea.
One who administers an oath without being appointed.
One who causes the destruction of the virility of animals.
In a dispute between father and son, the witnesses shall be fined ten paṇas.
And whoever should be between those two, for him the highest fine shall be imposed.
And for one who practices fraud with scales and measures.
And [the same applies] to one who sells counterfeit goods.
[The king shall confiscate] the merchandise of merchants who, having banded together, withhold it at an improper price.
And for those who sell [goods] individually; furthermore, he who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, shall be fined one hundred paṇas by the king.
Whatever loss occurs to one who does not purchase what has been sold shall belong to the purchaser alone.
For one who sells what has been prohibited by the king, there shall be confiscation of that property.
A ferryman who collects a land toll shall be fined ten paṇas.

A ferryman, a customs officer, or one who collects tolls [commit an offense] against those who are celibate students, forest-dwellers, mendicants, pregnant women, or those following a path to a sacred ford.
And he should give that to them.
In gambling, those who play with fraudulent dice shall have their hands cut off.
For those who play with the physical body as a stake, there is the cutting off of the pincers.

And for those who break open knots [of property], and for those who drive away [livestock], the hand shall be cut off. If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman is not present to guard them, it is the fault of the herdsman.
And he shall pay the value of the lost animal to its owner.
One who milks a cow that has not been authorized [to do so] shall pay twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
If a buffalo should cause the destruction of crops, its keeper shall be fined eight māṣas.
The lord of Apālā.
A horse, a camel, or a donkey.
If it is a cow, half of that [is the fine].
Half of that [is the fine for] goats and sheep.
When they have finished eating and are seated, it is double.
In all cases, the owner shall also pay the value of the destroyed crop.
There is no offense on a path, in a village, or at the edge of a pasture.
And in that which is unobstructed.
For a short time.
But he who should employ those of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who has abandoned the life of a renunciant shall perform service as a slave for the king.
A hired servant who abandons his service before the term is completed shall pay the full value of his wages.
And he shall be ordered to pay a fine of one hundred paṇas.
Whatever is destroyed through that fault shall belong to the owner.
Except in the case of an adverse stroke of fate.
If the master should dismiss the laborer before the term is completed, he must pay him the full value of his wages.
And one hundred paṇas to the king.
He who gives away a maiden already given to another shall be punished like a thief.
Except for the fault of the donor.
Abandoning that which is faultless.
And [he should give] his wife.
If one purchases another's property without knowing it to be so, there is no fault in that case for him.
The owner shall receive the property.
If one should purchase something that is unmanifested and of low value, then both the buyer and the seller shall be punished like thieves.
One who misappropriates the property of the community shall be banished.
And whoever should transgress that mutual understanding.
He shall be made to pay the creditor's wealth together with the interest on deposits, loans for use, and profits.
And he should be punished by the king like a thief.
And whoever should say that what was not set down was set down.
Having punished the breaker of the boundary with the highest amercement, he shall have the boundary established once again.
One who eats forbidden food that causes loss of caste shall be banished.
One who sells what is unfit for consumption or what is not to be sold, as well as one who breaks an image of a deity, shall be punished with the highest amercement.
A physician practicing falsely toward superior persons.
In the case of middling [offenses], the penance is middling.
First, among animals.
One who fails to deliver what has been promised shall, after being made to pay it, be fined the first amercement.
For false witnesses, the confiscation of all their property shall be carried out.
And for members of the assembly who subsist on bribes.
He who bestows upon another land measuring even a single cow-hide that has been pledged to someone else, without first releasing it from that person, is liable to capital punishment.
If it is less than sixteen suvarṇas, he shall be fined [the deficiency].
A man might eat alone for a year whatever fruit has been produced;

yet when two men dispute over a pledge that was deposited between them, the one whose possession of the fruit was established by force—provided it was done without compulsion—is the one to whom the fruit belongs.
But when property has been properly enjoyed for a long time with title, the possessor acquires it there; it can never be taken away from him.

Whatever property was enjoyed by the father according to custom and in accordance with dharma, when he has passed away, it need not be contested; for that which was acquired through enjoyment belongs to him.
Even in the absence of a written document, the fourth person shall obtain that [share] there.
In the killing of those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins, as well as elephants, horses, and others, the killer incurs no fault.
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin, one should indeed kill an approaching assassin without hesitation.
No fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer in the killing of an *ātatāyin* (one who seeks to kill).

One should know that there are seven types of *ātatāyins*: one with a raised sword, one with poison, fire, or a raised hand for a curse, one who kills by means of the *Atharvaveda*, a slanderer of kings, and one who violates another’s wife.
Others say that those who seize one's fame or wealth, as well as those who take away one's dharma or property, are also [to be considered] such.
I have described to you in brief the rules for punishment regarding all offenses, which would otherwise be too extensive to detail at length.
Regarding other offenses as well, having taken into account the caste, wealth, and age [of the offender], the king should determine the punishment after consulting with Brahmins.

One who releases a person deserving of punishment shall incur a fine double that of the offense; and one appointed [to administer justice] who punishes those not deserving of punishment is the lowest of men.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words, and no perpetrator of violence or one who strikes with a staff, shares in the world of Śakra.
Then the creditor shall recover from the debtor the amount of wealth that has been given as agreed.
Two, three, four, five, and a hundred [units] are [to be given] month by month according to the sequence of the castes.
Or all castes may pay interest according to their respective agreements.
Even if it has not been performed, it shall be done as prescribed upon the lapse of one year.
Except in the case of damage caused by the king or by fate, the creditor shall restore the pledge that has been destroyed.
Even when the increase of the end has entered.
An immovable pledge [is not valid] except by verbal agreement.
Whatever immovable property has been given solely for the purpose of securing the repayment of the money received, that shall be returned once the money received has been repaid.
When the principal amount lent has been paid and the creditor does not accept it, interest ceases to accrue from that point forward.
The maximum interest on gold is double the principal.
For grain, it is threefold.
For cloth, it is fourfold.
The [measure] of the juice is eightfold.
The lineage of women and cattle [is determined] by their mothers.
The ownership of yeast, cotton, thread, leather, weapons, bricks, and charcoal is inalienable.
For those not mentioned, the fine is double.
One who accomplishes a task undertaken for him in any way whatsoever should not be subject to reproach by the king.
If one being investigated should approach the king, he shall be punished with a fine equal to that [of the offense].
If the creditor approaches the king, the debtor, having been proven in that matter, shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the amount of the debt.
And a creditor who has recovered his debt shall receive a twentieth part [of the amount].
Even if one who denies everything is proven on only one point, he must pay the entire amount.
And its proofs are threefold: written documents, witnesses, and the performance of a formal agreement.
What has been received in the presence of witnesses should be returned only in the presence of witnesses.
When the person for whose benefit the document was written has entered [into the transaction], one should cause the document to be read.
In the case of an incomplete gift or when the document is not present, the creditor shall provide his own written acknowledgment.
If the creditor has died, has entered the religious order, or has been away abroad for twenty years, the debt must be paid by his sons or grandsons.
Beyond this, there is nothing for those who do not desire it.
Whether he has sons or is sonless, the inheritor of the estate shall pay the debt.
One who takes a wife from a man without wealth.
A woman does not [experience suffering] caused by her husband or her sons.
A husband and son do not owe a debt created by a woman.
The father does not [suffer] what was done by the son.
He who remains [in the family] shall pay the debt contracted by those who were undivided.
And the paternal debt belongs to brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance.
And they shall be divided into shares according to their inheritance.
And that which was done for the sake of the family.
He who, having received a loan in full with the agreement that he would repay it equally tomorrow, does not pay it later out of greed, shall likewise incur interest on it.
Suretyship is prescribed for appearance, for testimony, and for payment;
however, if the first two fail, they must be made to pay, and in the case of the latter, even their sons may be liable.

If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to the agreement; however, if no specific distinction has been made among them, the action shall proceed according to the will of the creditor.
Whatever amount the surety may have paid when pressured by the creditor, the debtor ought to pay that same amount doubled to the surety.
Now, written documents are of three kinds.
It is witnessed by the king, witnessed by others, and without witnesses.
A document executed in the royal court by a scribe appointed thereto, bearing the signature of its presiding officer, is one witnessed by the king.
Wherever and by whomever it may have been written, if it is marked with the signatures of the witnesses in their own hands, it is considered "with witnesses."
That which is written by one's own hand is without witnesses.
That which is performed under duress is not authoritative.
All [sufferings] are indeed produced by the substrates of existence.
Even if it is accompanied by witnesses, it is tainted by corrupted actions and marked by the suspicion of perjury.
And it was written by such a scribe.
And [an act] committed by a woman, a child, one who is not independent, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one who is terrified, or one who has been beaten.
That which is not contrary to local customs, whose characteristics are clearly defined by the qualified person, and whose sequence and syllables are unimpaired, is authoritative.
A document that is doubtful may be proven by means of its color, the marks made upon it, the paper itself, and logical arguments, as well as by other evidence consistent with those arguments.
Wherever the debtor, the creditor, the witness, or even the scribe dies, there that document shall be validated by their own handwriting.
Now, those who are not witnesses:

Nor [should one consult] a king, a Vedic scholar, an ascetic, a gambler, a thief, one who is dependent on others, a woman, a child, a rash person, one who is very old, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one who is accused of a crime, an outcast, one afflicted by hunger or thirst, one in distress, one who is blind with passion, or one who is blind.
And [the spies] who are enemies, friends, relatives, those connected by wealth, those engaged in forbidden acts, those whose faults have been observed, and their associates.
But one who, though not specifically designated as a witness, comes forward and speaks [should be accepted].
And one who is a single witness is not [admissible].
In cases of theft, violence, verbal or physical assault, and adultery, witnesses need not be examined.
Now, concerning witnesses.
Those of noble birth, endowed with good conduct and wealth, performers of sacrifices, ascetics, fathers of sons, knowers of dharma, students, truthful, and elders learned in the three Vedas.
Even a single person who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities and is approved by both parties [is sufficient].
When two parties are disputing, the witnesses of the one who brought the initial claim are to be questioned.
Where, due to the requirements of the case, the burden of proof (ādharyam) falls upon the proponent (pūrvapakṣin), there it also falls upon the opponent (prativādin).
If the designated witness has died or gone to another country, those who heard what was stated by him are the authority.
A witness is so called because of seeing or hearing [the matter] in person.
And witnesses are purified by truth.
Where there is the killing of those belonging to the [four] castes, there [the fault is removed] by untruth.
To purify that [sin], the twice-born should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.
A Śūdra shall give a morsel of food for one day to ten cows. One should recognize a false witness by a natural change in demeanor, a distortion of facial color, and incoherent speech.
And having summoned the witnesses at sunrise, he should question them after they have taken their oaths.
One should ask the Brahmin, "Speak."
"Speak the truth," [he says] to the Kṣatriya.
A Vaiśya [should be approached] with cattle, grain, or gold.
But for all great mortal sins (mahāpātaka), [the penance applies] to a Śūdra.
And he should cause the witnesses to hear [the charges].
Whatever worlds belong to those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), and whatever belong to those who have committed minor sins (upapātakin), those belong likewise to false witnesses.
By truth the sun shines.
By truth the moon shines.
By truth the wind blows.
By truth, the earth is sustained.
By truth the waters stand firm.
By truth, Agni [is established].
And the sky by truth.
By truth, the gods [prosper].
By truth, sacrifices [are established].
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale; indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.

"For those who, though knowing [the truth], remain silent and indifferent when called to testify, are equal to false witnesses in their sin and likewise in their punishment. Thus indeed should the king question the witnesses according to the order of their castes."
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
for him who asserts otherwise, defeat is certain.

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, O Lord of Men, the king should accept the majority; if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.
In whatever legal dispute a false witness should speak untruth, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been accomplished, it shall be as if unaccomplished.
Now follows the performance of the ritual pledge.
In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [the punishment] shall be according to his will.
In cases of deposit and theft, the value of the object determines the penalty.
For all categories of goods, one should determine the value in terms of gold.
In that case, if the cloth is black, one should cause a Śūdra to swear an oath with dūrvā grass in his hand.
For two *kṛṣṇalas*, the fine is one *tila*.
When the three black lines are at the bottom, it is the Rajatakara.
For four kṛṣṇalas, the fine is one suvarṇa.
When the five black [planets] are in their respective signs, he is one who has raised the earth with his plow.
For a Śūdra, a fine of half a suvarṇa less than the treasury-fee (kośa) shall be imposed; beyond that, one of the ordeals—by the balance, fire, water, or poison—shall be administered as appropriate.
If the value is double, the same agreements as previously stated apply to the Vaiśya.
For a Kṣatriya, it is threefold.
For a Brahmin, [the staff] is four cubits long, excluding the handle.
One should not give a treasury to a brahmin.
Except for the performance of an act that binds one to a future time and occasion.
In the section on the treasury, one should cause the Brahmin who has ploughed the earth with a furrow of water to swear an oath.
Even in a minor matter, one should cause a person whose faults have been previously observed to undergo one of the divine ordeals.
What is known by the virtuous is true conduct, even if it does not lead to a great purpose.
The plaintiff shall pay the court fee.
And one who is accused shall undergo an ordeal.
In cases of treason against the king or acts of violence, [the ordeal may be administered] even without the turning of the head.
The balance should be administered for women, Brahmins, the deformed, the infirm, and the sick.
And that [fragrance] does not waft when there is no wind.
Fire must not be given to lepers, the infirm, or blacksmiths.
And during autumn and summer.
Poison must not be administered to lepers, those afflicted with bile disorders, or Brahmins.
And during the rainy season.
Water [should not be given] to those afflicted by phlegmatic diseases, to the timid, to those suffering from asthma and coughing, nor to those who live by water.
And during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira.
The treasury must not be given to atheists.
Nor in a region afflicted by disease or pestilence.
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on, he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the gods and Brahmins.
Now, the ordeal by balance.
It is four cubits high and two cubits long.
Therein, the balance-beam is made from a strong wood, five cubits in length, with a scale-pans suspended on both ends.
And any one among the goldsmiths or brazier-workers should maintain her.
Having made two counter-men of equal weight and well-marked, one should cause the man to descend.
And one should take up the ordeal according to the established rule.
And Tulādhāra.
Those worlds which are ordained for the slayers of Brahmins, and those worlds for false witnesses—
by means of these synonymous terms for dharma, you are called the "Dhaṭa" (the Balance).
O Dhaṭa, you alone know those things which mortals do not perceive.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed upon you; therefore, you ought to deliver him from this doubt in accordance with Dharma."
Then he should place that man on the scale once again; if, when weighed, he increases [in weight], then he is pure according to the law.
If the sling breaks or the axle snaps, he should place the man on it again;
then [he should test him with] fire.
One should construct seven mandalas with an interval of sixteen finger-breadths each.
Then, while he is facing eastward with both arms extended, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in his hands.
And one should wrap those two hands together with a thread.
Then, one should place there an iron ball of fifty palas, heated to the color of fire and made smooth.
Taking that [staff], he should walk neither too quickly nor too slowly, placing his feet within the [prescribed] circles.
Then, having passed over the seventh circle, one should drop a lump of iron upon the ground.
One whose hands are burnt in any part should be declared impure;
however, that man who is not burnt at all shall be pure.
But if one should cause [the accused] to fall out of fear, or if he is burnt and not clearly perceived, one should make him carry the metal again because the oath has not been purified.

Having consecrated a lump of iron with this mantra, he should then place it in the man's hands: "O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness; O Agni, you alone know those things which human beings do not know."
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification; therefore, you ought to rescue him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Then water.
In water that is free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like;
Therein, having grasped the knees of another man who is submerged up to his navel and free from disease or hatred, one should enter the consecrated water.
And at that same moment, another person should discharge an arrow with a bow that is neither too harsh nor too soft.
And another man would quickly retrieve that arrow.
For otherwise, it would be impure even upon the perception of a single factor.
You move within the waters of all beings like a witness; you alone understand those waters which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, is sinking into you; therefore, you ought to rescue him from this peril according to dharma."
Now, regarding poison:
All poisons are not to be given away.
Except for the Śārṅga bow produced from the Himālaya mountains.
And one should give seven mouthfuls of barley soaked in ghee to the accused person.
If the poison, free from its force and exhaustion, is digested easily, then knowing it to be pure, one should dismiss it at the end of the day.
Because of its toxicity and its uneven nature, you are cruel to all embodied beings;
O Poison, you alone know those things which human beings do not perceive.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification; therefore, you ought to rescue him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma.
Now, the treasury.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should drink three handfuls of the water from their ablutions.
Saying, "This was not done by me," he faces the deity who has been installed.

If, within two weeks or even three weeks, one should see [the signs] for him, one should know him to be impure; conversely, in the opposite case, he is pure. And a righteous king should honor a man who has been proven pure by the ordeal.
Now, there are twelve sons.
The first is the legitimate son of the body (aurasa), who is begotten by oneself upon one's own wedded wife.
The second is the *kṣetraja* son, begotten by a sapinda relative or by a man of a higher caste upon a woman who has been duly appointed.
The third is the son of a daughter.
She who was given by her father with the stipulation, "The son who is born of her shall be my son," is a *putrikā*.
Even without the formal rite of appointment as a *putrikā*, a daughter who has been bestowed [in marriage] while being without a brother is indeed a *putrikā*.
The fourth is rebirth.
One who has been consecrated again while still intact is a *punarbhū*.
Furthermore, even one who has not been previously married is considered "one whose former husband was another."
The fifth is the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna).
He was begotten by one who had not been consecrated while still in his father's house.
And that belongs to the one who took her hand in marriage.
And the sixth is one born in secret within the household.
He belongs to the one from whose bed he was born.
The son born of a woman pregnant at marriage is the seventh.
The son belongs to her who is consecrated while pregnant.
And that belongs to the one who took her hand in marriage.
And the adopted son is the eighth.
And he was given by his parents to whomever [they chose].
And the ninth is one who has been purchased.
And he by whom it was purchased.
The tenth [member] is that which has approached spontaneously.
And he approached him.
The discarded son is the eleventh.
He was abandoned by both his father and his mother.
And he by whom it was grasped.
And wherever it is produced, it is the twelfth.
Among these, each preceding one is superior to the next.
He alone is the heir to the inheritance.
And he should support others as well.
For those who are unmarried, he should perform the sacramental rite in accordance with his own means.
But those who are outcasts, eunuchs, those with incurable diseases, or those who are physically deformed do not receive a share.
They must be maintained by those who inherit their property.
And their sons born of wives of equal status are the heirs of the share, but not the son of one who has fallen from caste.
But when an action leading to defeat has been committed, they arise immediately thereafter.
And those born of women in the inverse order of castes are also non-partakers [of the inheritance].
His sons [have authority] even over the property inherited from their grandfather.
Those who take shares must be supported by them.
And he who takes the wealth is the one who offers the funeral rice-ball.
Even among women married one after another, the son of one is indeed the son of all.
And among brothers born of the same father.
Even if he does not obtain his father's wealth, the son should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put, he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality, provided that he beholds the face of the born son while it is still living.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity; and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
In this world, no distinction is found between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers a man who has no son, just like a son’s son.
Sons born of women of the same caste are of the same caste as their fathers.
In marriages in the natural order, the offspring are of the same caste as the mother.
In that regard, the son of a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra father is an Āyogava.
The Pulkasa and the Māgadha are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman by a Vaiśya and a Śūdra respectively.
And the Caṇḍāla, the Vaidehaka, and the Sūta are the sons of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and a Kṣatriya, respectively.
And the mixtures of mixtures are also incalculable.
The entry onto the stage for the Āyogavas.
The Pulkasas are hunters.
The practice of offering praise is characteristic of the Magadhas.
And the execution of those condemned to death belongs to the Caṇḍālas.
The protection of women and their livelihood are the duties of the Vaidehakas.
The management of horses and chariots is the duty of charioteers.
The specific distinction for Caṇḍālas is that they must dwell outside the village and wear the clothes of the deceased.
And for all of them, marriage shall be with those of the same caste.
These castes arising from intermixture, as shown by their fathers and mothers—
whether they are concealed or manifest— are to be known by their own respective actions.

The unconditioned sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, as well as in the rescue of women, children, and others, is the cause of success for those who follow external paths.
If a father divides his sons, he may do so according to his own will regarding property acquired by himself.
But regarding ancestral property, the ownership of father and son is equal.
Those who have divided the paternal estate shall give a share to one born after the partition.
The property of one who dies without a son goes to the wife.
In his absence, it goes to the father.
In his absence, it goes to the mother.
In his absence, it goes to the brother.
In his absence, it goes to the brother's son.
In the absence of that, it goes to the relatives.
In the absence of that, it goes to the *sakulya*.
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to a fellow student.
In the absence of such heirs, the property—excluding that belonging to a Brāhmaṇa—reverts to the king.
The welfare of the brahmins is for the sake of the brahmins.
The preceptor shall take the property of a forest-dweller.
Or a disciple.

But a reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of a reunited coparcener; likewise, a uterine brother shall do so for a uterine brother, both for one who has been born and for one who has died.

What is given by the father, mother, son, or brother, and what is received as a subsequent gift (anvādheya)—this is the woman’s property (strīdhana). In the case of the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma form, if she dies childless, it belongs to her husband.
And in the remaining cases, the father shall take [the property].
In all these cases, whatever wealth exists at the time of her delivery belongs to the daughter.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their status.
But for those who have many fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father;

whatever paternal inheritance belongs to one, he shall take that, and not the other. If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons from wives of the four castes, they shall divide the paternal inheritance into ten parts.
In that case, the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take four shares.
The son of a Kṣatriya woman [inherits] three [shares].
The son of a Vaiśya woman receives two shares.
But the son of a Śūdra woman [inherits] one share.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have three sons, excluding one who is a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into nine parts.
They shall take shares divided into four, three, and two portions respectively, according to the order of their castes.
Excluding the Vaiśya, they should divide [the estate] into eight parts and take four, three, and one respectively.
Excluding the Kṣatriya, it is divided sevenfold: four, two, and one.
Excluding the Brāhmaṇas, it is divided into six groups: three, two, and one.
For a Kṣatriya, this same division applies among the sons born of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra wife.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya,
then from the wealth divided into seven parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares.
A member of the royal caste [should offer] three.
Now, if there are two [sons], a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya,
then the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares out of the estate divided into six parts.
A Vaiśya shall receive two shares.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, one a Brāhmaṇa and the other a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into five parts.
But the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares.
A Śūdra [should give] one.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons who are a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, then they should divide that wealth into five parts.
But the Kṣatriya shall take three shares.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, one a Kṣatriya and the other a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into four parts.
But the Kṣatriya shall take three shares.
A Śūdra [should offer] one.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya should have two sons who are a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into three parts.
The Vaiśya, however, shall take two shares.
A Śūdra [should give] one.
Now, the sons of a Brāhmaṇa who has only one son—whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas—are entitled to inherit the entire estate.
For a Kṣatriya, they are a Rājanya and a Vaiśya.
A Vaiśya [should approach] a Vaiśya woman.
A Śūdra [is the heir] of a Śūdra.

Among the twice-born, however, a Śūdra son alone shall take half the inheritance. As for the estate of one who leaves no son, the mothers shall receive shares in accordance with the shares of their sons.
And daughters who are unmarried.
Sons of the same caste shall take equal shares.
They should give the eldest an additional share as the best portion.

If there should be two sons of a Brāhmaṇī and one son of a Śūdrā, then, from the property divided into nine parts, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇī shall take eight shares and the son of the Śūdrā shall take one share.
Now, if there should be two sons by a Śūdra woman and one son by a Brāhmaṇa woman,
then the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares of the property divided into six parts,
while the two Śūdra sons shall take two shares.
In this manner, the conceptualization of parts occurs elsewhere as well.
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that instance.
Whatever one may acquire through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
that which is obtained by one's own effort, he need not give away unless he so desires.
But when one recovers ancestral property that was previously unobtained, he need not share it with his sons if he so desires, as it is self-acquired.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession, pasture land, and books are not to be divided.
One should not have a deceased twice-born person carried out by a Śūdra.
A twice-born man shall not [initiate] a Śūdra.
The sons shall carry out the father and the mother.
Śūdras do not [serve] a Brāhmaṇa, even if he be their father.
Those Brahmins who carry out the funeral rites for a destitute Brahmin shall partake in the heavenly world.
Having carried out the deceased relative and performed the cremation rites, they should approach the funeral pyre from the left and, still wearing their clothes, perform an immersion in water.
Having performed the pouring of water for the deceased, they should offer a single funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass.
Having changed their garments and bitten neem leaves, they should enter the house after placing a footprint upon a stone at the doorway.
And they should throw unbroken grains into the fire.
On the fourth day, they should perform the collection of the bones.
Their casting into the waters of the Ganges.
For as many thousands of years as the bones of a man remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that long he dwells in the heavenly world.
For as long as the period of impurity lasts, they should offer water and one funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased.
And they should subsist on food that has been purchased or obtained.
And they were abstainers from meat.
They sleep on the bare ground.
And those who sleep separately.

Having departed from the village at the end of the period of impurity, having had their hair and beards shaved, having bathed with a paste of sesame or a paste of mustard seeds, and having changed their clothes, they shall enter their home.
Having performed the rite of pacification there, they should also perform the worship of the Brahmins.
The gods are the invisible gods; the brahmins are the visible gods.
The worlds are sustained by the Brahmins.
By the grace of the brahmins, the deities abide in heaven;
the word spoken by a brahmin never becomes false anywhere.
Whatever the Brahmins, being most satisfied, declare, that the deities welcome;
when they are satisfied, the deities who dwell beyond the senses are constantly satisfied with those deities who are visible.

Those of undaunted spirit should offer consolation to those afflicted by suffering whose kinsmen have died; O Earth, delightful to the mind, I shall now declare to you those words with which they should do so.
That which is the northern course is the day of the gods.
The southern course of the sun is night.
A year is a day and night.
Thirty of those [days] constitute a month.
Twelve months constitute a year.
The Kali Yuga consists of twelve hundred divine years.
The Dvāpara age has twice [the duration], and the Tretā age has thrice [the duration].
The Kṛtayuga consists of four such qualities.
Twelve thousand divine years constitute a cycle of four ages (caturyuga).
Seventy-one cycles of four yugas constitute a manvantara.
And a thousand cycles of four yugas is a kalpa.
And that is the day of the grandfather.
And his night is of the same duration.
By calculating months and years through such days and nights, the lifespan of the entire Brahmā is one hundred years.
And a human day is delimited by the lifespan of a Brahmā.
At its end is a great eon (mahākalpa).
His night lasts for exactly that long.
There is no counting at all for the human days and nights that have passed.
Nor does it exist for those yet to come.
Because time is without beginning or end.
Thus, in this supportless time that flows on incessantly, I do not perceive any such entity whose stability could be permanent.
As many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges or drops of rain when Indra pours it down,
so do fourteen lords of the gods perish in each kalpa, as well as the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of the Daityas have perished here through time; what then can be said of mortal men?
And many royal sages, endowed with all virtues, as well as gods and celestial seers, have met their end in the course of time.
Even those who are capable of being the cause of creation and destruction in this world are led away by time; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Overwhelmed by time, every living being is led to the next world, subject to the noose of karma; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no help to be found in this world.
Since grieving people do not benefit the deceased here in this world, one should certainly not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
For one who departs with both good deeds and evil deeds as his two companions, what need has he for kinsmen, whether they grieve or not?
Until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed, one who has died remains a *preta*;
having reached the world of the ancestors, he eats at the *śrāddha* food that is equal to the *svadhā* offering.
Therefore, offer the *śrāddha* for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
And likewise, in the human state, he receives the ancestral offerings (śrāddha) given by his own kinsmen.
When a śrāddha is performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer is certain; therefore, having abandoned useless grief, one should always perform the śrāddha.
This much alone should always be done for a deceased person by his kinsmen; a man should not help either the deceased or himself by grieving.
Seeing that the world is without refuge and that even one's kinsmen die, O men, always choose the Dharma alone as your companion.
Even a kinsman, once dead, is unable to follow the deceased man; for, with the exception of a wife, the path to Yama is closed to everyone else.
Dharma alone follows him wherever he goes;
indeed, in this essence-less world of men, practice Dharma without delay.
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished.
Death seizes and departs with one who is attached to fields, shops, and houses, and whose mind is directed elsewhere, just as a she-wolf carries off a lamb.
Time has no one dear to it, nor is there anyone it hates; when the lifespan resulting from one's karma is exhausted, it forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings, nor repeated recitations can protect a human being who has been overtaken by death or even by old age.
For one is not able to ward off an impending misfortune even by means of hundreds of precautions; what lamentation can there be in that regard?
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so too does previously performed karma certainly find its doer.
Beings have an unmanifest beginning and a manifest middle;
just as in this body the embodied self passes through childhood, youth, and old age, so too does it attain another body— the wise man is not deluded by this.
Just as a person here takes up a garment after discarding one previously worn, so too does the embodied being take up a new body bound by karma.
Weapons do not cut this, fire does not burn it, waters do not moisten it, and the wind does not dry it.
This [Self] is neither to be cut, nor to be burnt, neither to be moistened nor to be dried.
It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. It is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable;
therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.

Then, upon the passing of the period of impurity, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as he is able, facing northward, honored with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and other such things.

In a rite for a single deceased person (ekoddiṣṭa), one should modify the mantras to the singular; in the vicinity of the food remnants, one should offer a single rice-ball (piṇḍa) by means of that person’s name and lineage.

When the Brahmins have finished eating and have been honored with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should offer inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) addressed by the name and lineage of the deceased; then he should make three trenches, four finger-breadths wide, that deep, and one span long, with intervals between them equal to their width.
Having kindled three fires near the furrows and strewn grass around them, he should offer three oblations into each one.
To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! Homage!
To Agni Kavyavāhana, the bearer of offerings to the ancestors, svadhā! Homage!
To Yama, to Aṅgiras, Svadhā! Homage!
And at the three places, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) as before.
Having filled three pits with rice, curd, ghee, honey, and meat, one should mutter the mantra "etat te" (this for you).
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] every month on the anniversary of the death.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins, preceded by offerings to the gods, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
In this [rite], one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and the water for the feet (pādya).
With the mantra "May the earth unite with you, and the common [waters]," he should join the water from the guest's *pādya* vessel into the three *pitṛ* *pādya* vessels.
One should offer four pindas in the vicinity of the leavings.
And having followed the Brahmins who have sipped water and received their sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them.
Then, one should place the *preta*-piṇḍa among the three piṇḍas, just like the water from the vessel for the feet (*pādya*).
Even when in close proximity to three furrows, it is exactly the same.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed like the monthly *māsika* offerings; having performed the *śrāddha* for twelve days, one should perform it on the thirteenth day.
For Śūdras, however, [the rite] takes place on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras.
If an intercalary month should occur within the year, then one should increase the period for the monthly offering by one day.
The sapindikarana rite for women should be performed in exactly the same manner; likewise, one should perform the śrāddha every year as long as one lives.
For one whose sapindikarana has been performed before the completion of a year, one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of a year.
For a Brāhmaṇa, there is a ten-day period of impurity (āśauca) upon the birth or death of his sapinda relatives.
For a Kṣatriya, it lasts twelve days.
For a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days.
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] one month.
And the sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person.
During a period of ritual impurity, fire-offerings, giving, receiving, and Vedic study are suspended.
During a period of impurity, one should not eat the food of anyone.
If one eats food even once from a Brāhmaṇa or others who are in a state of impurity, his own impurity lasts for as long as theirs.
Upon the removal of the impurity, one should perform the expiation.

If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a person of his own caste, he should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
But during the period of impurity for a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by fasting and performing this very same rite.
And a Kṣatriya [is impure] during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya.
During the period of impurity for a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
During the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and during the period of impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya should go to a flowing river and mutter the Gāyatrī five hundred times.
And a Vaiśya, during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a Śūdra should perform a bath during the period of impurity of the twice-born.
A Śūdra, having bathed during the period of impurity for a Śūdra, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For wives and slaves, the period of impurity is equal to that of their master, according to their respective order of birth.
When the master has died, it belongs to himself.
For those of lower caste who have committed an offense against sapiṇḍas of higher caste, purification occurs at the end of that [latter's] period of impurity.
For a Brāhmaṇa, among Sapinda relatives who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods of impurity are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively.
For a Kṣatriya [impurity resulting from the death] of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra lasts for six nights or three nights respectively.
For a Vaiśya among Śūdras, purification occurs in six nights.
In the case of a miscarriage, the penance consists of days and nights equal in number to the months [of gestation].
In the case of a birth or a death occurring within the family, purification is immediate.
If a child who has not yet cut its teeth dies, the impurity lasts for only that very day.
For him there is no consecration by fire, nor the rite of water-libation.
But for one whose teeth have appeared but who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony performed, purification occurs after one day and night.
But if the tonsure ceremony has been performed, yet the other rites have not been completed, purification occurs after three nights.
Thereafter, at the time as previously stated.
For women, marriage is the purificatory rite (saṃskāra).
In the case of women who have been consecrated [in marriage], there is no period of impurity for the paternal kin.
If her birth or death should occur while she is in her father’s house, then the impurity lasts for one night and three nights, respectively.
If another birth-impurity should occur during the midst of a birth-impurity, then purification occurs upon the cessation of the first impurity.
At the end of the night, [it is accomplished] in two days.
In three days, at dawn.
Likewise, if a death occurs among one's kinsmen during a period of impurity caused by another death, the same rule applies.
One staying in another country, upon hearing [of a birth or death], shall become pure by means of the remainder of the period of impurity.
When the period of impurity has passed, however, at the end of a year, purification occurs after one night.
After that, by means of bathing.
When both the teacher and the maternal grandfather have passed away, [the purification occurs] after three nights.
When sons born of other than one's own loins have been born or have died, and when wives who previously had another husband have given birth or have died;
In the case of the death of the teacher's wife, a son, a sub-teacher, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a fellow student, or a pupil, one must observe impurity for one night.
And also when a person who is not a sapinda has died in one's own house.
There is no period of impurity for those killed by Bhṛgu, fire, fasting, water, battle, lightning, or a king.
Nor [should one recite] during the king's work of anointing.
Nor [is it a fault] for those observing vows when they are engaged in their vow.
Nor [is it a fault] for artisans in their artisanal work.
It does not apply to those who carry out the king's commands by his will.
Nor [should one study] during the consecration of a deity or at a wedding, provided these have been previously prepared.
Not when there is confusion regarding the location.
And even in times of dire distress.
Those who commit suicide and those who are outcasts do not participate in the impurity rites or the water libations.
On the day of death, the slave-girl of one who has fallen [from caste] should overturn a jar of water with her foot.
He who cuts the noose of one who has died by hanging is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
And he who performs the funeral rites for those who have sacrificed their own lives.
And he who causes the shedding of tears [for him].
For every deceased person, having shed tears together with their relatives, [one should perform purification] by means of bathing.
If the collection of bones has not been performed, [one is purified] by bathing with one's clothes on.

A twice-born man, having followed the funeral procession of a Śūdra corpse, should go to a river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
One hundred and eight [recitations] for a deceased twice-born man.
A Śūdra, having followed a deceased person, should perform a ritual bath.
Upon inhaling the smoke from a funeral pyre, all castes should perform a ritual bath.
After sexual intercourse, a bad dream, when blood has come to the throat, and after vomiting or purging.
And also when the work of shaving has been performed.
And having touched one who has touched a corpse, as well as a menstruating woman, a Caṇḍāla, or a sacrificial post (yūpa).
Except for edible [five-toed animals], one should avoid the carcasses of five-toed animals and the fat from their bones.
In all these ritual baths, one should not wear a garment that has not been washed.
A menstruating woman becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
Having touched a menstruating woman of a lower caste, or having been touched by a menstruating woman, one shall not eat until she has become purified.
