Having touched a woman of the same caste or of a higher caste, one becomes pure immediately after bathing.

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or desired to eat or study; having drunk, bathed, spat, put on a garment, walked upon a road, voided urine or excrement, or touched the bone of a five-toed animal that is not oily, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
And [it is a fault] in conversing with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas.
If one is defiled by bodily impurities below the navel or on the forearms, or by wine and intoxicants, that limb shall be purified by washing it with earth and water.
If it has been defiled elsewhere, one should wash that limb with earth and water and then perform a bath.
But if it has been defiled by contact with the mouth, one should fast and bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And [the body] is struck by the lips of the teeth. Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nails, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from honey (mādhvī), and that made from flour (paiṣṭī).
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the twice-born.
Mādhūka, aikṣava, ṭāṅka, kaula, khārjūra, and pānasa—
these ten intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them.
A disciple, however, performing the funeral rites for his deceased guru, becomes purified there in ten nights along with those who partake of the food offered to the deceased.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.
One who has been initiated shall not perform the water-libation rite until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with cow-dung], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Of all forms of purity, purity regarding food is declared to be supreme;
for he who is pure in regard to food is truly pure, not he who is merely purified by earth and water.
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts are purified by charity;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by the recitation of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas are purified by austerity.
That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman whose mind is defiled is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This decision regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the decision concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.
That which is defiled by bodily impurities, by fermented liquors, or by intoxicants is said to be "extremely defiled."
Every iron vessel that has been utterly defiled shall be purified by being cast into fire.
One made of jewels, one made of stone, and one made of lotus-root are purified by burying them in the earth for seven nights.
One should discard that which is made of wood or clay.
If a garment that is utterly ruined becomes free of stains when washed, one should cut it away.
Objects made of gold, silver, lotus, or gems, which are not subject to staining, are purified by water.
Of the stone cups, the chalices, and the vessels.
The *caru* pot, the *sruc* ladle, and the *sruva* spoon [are cleansed] with hot water; during the sacrificial rite, the sacrificial vessels [are cleansed] by wiping them with the hand.
By sprinkling water upon the wooden sword, the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar.
And of beds, vehicles, and seats.
And [the same applies] when there are many [offenders].
And [the same applies] to grains, skins, ropes, woven cloth, bamboo mats, thread, and cotton garments.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, fruits, and flowers.
And of grass, wood, and dry leaves.
By the washing away of these.
And [the same applies] to those who are few.
Silk and woolen cloth [are purified] by means of alkaline substances.
With *ariṣṭaka* fruits for the *kutapa* goats.
Of silken cloths, with *śrīphala* fruits.
For linen garments, [the purification is] with white mustard seeds.
And [the same applies] to those made of horn, bone, or ivory.
[The purification] of deer-hair [cloths] is by means of lotus seeds.
For those made of copper, brass, tin, and lead, [the purification is] with acidic water.
With ashes, [one should purify] bell-metal and iron.
By means of carving, [the form] of wooden objects [is produced].
With cow-hair brushes for those made from fruit.
By sprinkling, [the purification] of things that are joined together [is accomplished].
For liquids, purification is by straining; for large quantities of sugarcane products such as molasses and the like kept in the house, it is by sprinkling with water and fire.
And of all salts.
Furthermore, earthenware vessels [are purified] by re-firing.
By re-consecrating images of deities that have been purified like material objects.
Of the food that has not been prepared, one should discard only that portion which is defiled and perform the threshing and washing of the remainder.
Food prepared in an amount exceeding one *droṇa* does not become defiled even if it is contaminated.

Having removed only that which is defiled, one should pour gold-infused water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra over it; furthermore, one should show it to a goat and to fire. That which has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed at, and that which is defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth.

One should draw out all the water and purify the remainder with a cloth. In a well constructed with baked bricks, one should kindle a fire; subsequently, in a well filled with fresh water, one should deposit the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
O Earth, in the case of small, stagnant reservoirs, purification is said to be like that of a well; however, there is no such defect in large ones.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by word.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise that has been displayed for sale; so too are almsfood offered by a Brāhmaṇa and all mining sites.

The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game. The meat of an animal killed by dogs is declared to be pure, as is that of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, by Cāṇḍālas and the like, or by robbers.
One should declare those apertures of the body that are above the navel to be pure;
those below it are impure, as are the excretions that have fallen from the body.
Flies, droplets of water, shadows, a cow, an elephant, a horse, rays of light, dust, earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure.
The primary [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants; nor do droplets that fall upon the body; nor do the beard hairs that have entered the mouth; nor what is caught between the teeth.

Drops that touch the feet of one who is giving water for rinsing to others are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. However, if one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled, [the purification is as follows]:

a house is purified by sweeping and smearing; a book by sprinkling; the earth by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, scraping, burning, or by the dwelling of cows. Cows are pure and auspicious; in cows, the worlds are established.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all evil. Cow-urine, cow-dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and the yellow pigment (rocanā)—[these are the products of the cow].
This water from the horns of cows is the supreme sixfold auspiciousness; it is the most excellent among the products of cows, meritorious, and the destroyer of all sins.
Scratching the bodies of cows indeed destroys all impurities; by giving morsels of food to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world.

For the Gaṅgā dwells here in the footprint of cows; likewise, nourishment is increased by their dust; prosperity resides in their dried dung, and merit in bowing to them; therefore, one should constantly offer salutation to them.
Now, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives according to the order of the castes.
There are three for a Kṣatriya.
There are two for a Vaiśya.
One for a Śūdra.
Among them, when marrying a woman of the same caste, the hand should be taken in marriage.
In the case of marrying a girl of a different caste, a Kṣatriya girl [should impose] an arrow.
A goad [is the emblem] of a Vaiśya maiden.
[He was] within the hem of the garment [of the king] by means of a Śūdra maiden.

One should not take as a wife a woman who is of the same lineage (*sagotrā*) or who shares the same ancestral seers (*samānārṣapravarā*). She must not be within five generations on the mother’s side, nor within seven generations on the father’s side.
Of the Nākulīs.
Nor one who is diseased.
Nor one with an extra limb.
Nor one who has a missing limb.
Nor one that is excessively tawny.
Nor one who is talkative.
Now, there are eight forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, the Gāndharva, the Āsura, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca.
The Brāhma marriage consists of inviting a virtuous man and giving a daughter to him.
The divine [offering] is for the officiating priest at the sacrifice.
By the mention of the "pair of cattle," it is the *ārṣa* form [of marriage].
By granting what is requested, one becomes like Prajāpati.
The Gāndharva form of marriage is the union of two people who both desire each other, but in the absence of their parents.
An Asura [is born] through purchase.
The Rākṣasa [is won] by taking her in battle.
The Paiśāca rite consists of approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated.
Among these, the first four are lawful.
The Gāndharva [form of marriage] is also [permitted] for Kṣatriyas.
The son of a Brāhmaṇī purifies twenty-one men.
The son of Daivī was Caturdaśa.
And there are seven sons of the Ṛṣis.
The Prājāpatya penance lasts for four days.
By giving a daughter in marriage according to the Brāhma rite, one causes her to go to the world of Brahmā.
By fate, one attains heaven.
The Vaiṣṇava [rite] is performed according to the Ṛṣi tradition.
By the Prājāpatya [rite], one reaches the world of the gods.
By the Gāndharva rite, one goes to the world of the Gandharvas.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, the maternal grandfather, and the mother are the givers of a maiden.
In the absence of the preceding one, each subsequent [teacher] is established in his natural state.
A maiden should choose her own husband only after having observed three menstrual periods;
once three periods have passed, she is always empowered to act for herself.
A maiden who sees her menses while still uninitiated in her father’s house [is considered fallen].
Now follow the duties of women.
The practice of observing vows identical to those of her husband.
The honoring of one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, teachers, deities, and guests.
The state of having well-maintained utensils.
The state of having hands that are never empty [of giving].
The state of keeping one's belongings well-secured.
A lack of delight in fundamental activities.
Dedication to the practice of auspicious conduct.
When the husband has gone abroad, she should refrain from the practice of personal adornment.
Not visiting the houses of others.
Not remaining in the vicinity of doors or windows.
Lack of autonomy in all actions.
Even in childhood, youth, and old age, there is dependence upon the father, the husband, and the son, respectively.
When her husband has died, she should observe celibacy or ascend the funeral pyre after him.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by serving her husband, however, she is exalted in heaven.
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living, she takes away his life-span and goes to hell.
Even though she is childless, she goes to heaven, just like those celibate students.
When there are many wives of the same caste, he should perform religious duties together with the eldest wife.
And in the case of mixed castes, even with a woman of the lowest rank who is of the same varna.
But in the absence of a woman of the same caste, [he may marry] one of the next lower caste, even if she belongs to the Āpadi category.
But a twice-born man must never [beget a son] by means of a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra woman can never be the wife of a twice-born man for the sake of dharma;
she is declared to be for his pleasure alone, for him who is blinded by passion.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth quickly lead their families, along with their descendants, to the status of Śūdras.
But for one whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are dominated by that [meat], the ancestors and gods do not eat, and he does not go to heaven.
The rite of impregnation (niṣekakarma) is performed when there is clear knowledge of the embryo's presence.
The *puṃsavana* rite is performed before the quickening of the fetus.
The parting of the hair ceremony is performed in the sixth or eighth month [of pregnancy].
And when the boy was born, the birth-rite was performed.
The naming ceremony shall take place at the end of the period of impurity.
Auspiciousness belongs to the Brahmin.
It belongs to a powerful Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, it should be provided with wealth.
That which is despised by a Śūdra.
In the fourth month, the showing of the sun.
In the sixth [month], the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.
In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed.
These very same rites for women are performed without mantras.
Their marriage is accompanied by mantras.
The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year from conception.
In the eleventh month from conception for a king.
The Vaiśyas [should initiate] in the twelfth year from conception.
For them, the girdles are made of muñja grass, bowstring, or balbaja grass, and consist of muñja grass.
The sacred threads and garments may be made of cotton, hemp, or wool.
The staffs are made of Palāśa, Khadira, or Udumbara wood.
The hairline, the forehead, and the nose are equal [in measure].
Or rather, all [of them] indeed.
They are straight and possess their bark.
Wandering for alms at the beginning of the day, in the middle of the day, and at the end of the day.
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this point, all three of these, if not consecrated at the proper time, become fallen from the Sāvitrī, Vrātyas, despised by the Āryas.
Whatever skin, whatever sacred thread, and whatever girdle are prescribed for him, and whatever staff and whatever garment—each of these remains his even during his vows.
Having cast the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
Now follows the residence in the teacher's house for those practicing the life of a religious student.
The practice of the two twilights.
One should recite the morning twilight prayer while standing, and the evening twilight prayer while seated.
The performance of the consecration and fire rituals occurs at two times.
Submerging like a staff in water.
Studying when summoned.
Acting for the pleasure and welfare of the guru.
The wearing of the girdle, staff, deerskin, and sacred thread.
Except for the house of one's teacher, he should go about begging alms from those who possess virtuous qualities.
The consumption of almsfood authorized by the guru.
One should avoid salt and fermented liquids prepared for ancestral rites, stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, food remnants, injury to living beings, and vulgar speech.
Sleeping on a low bed.
One should rise before the guru and go to rest after him.
And having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana), he should perform the salutation to the teacher (gurvabhivādana).
And with his hands crossed, he should touch his feet.
The right [eye] with the right [hand], and the other [eye] with the other [hand].
And at the conclusion of the salutation, he should announce his own name, ending with the word "bhoḥ."
Whether he is standing, sitting, lying down, eating, or facing away, one should not engage him in conversation.

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is walking; going forward to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running after, one should attend to one who is running.
Facing one who has turned his back.
Having approached the presence of one who is far away.
Having prostrated before him while he was lying down.
And within his range of vision, he should not sit as he pleases.
And one should not utter his name alone.
One should not imitate his gait, gestures, speech, and so forth.
He should not remain in a place where he would be subjected to censure or slander.
He should not remain on a single seat.
Except for stone slabs, wooden planks, and boats.
When the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher.
And unless instructed by his own teacher, he should not pay homage to his [other] teachers.
A student should behave toward a fellow student of equal age, a teacher, or the son of a teacher as he would toward his own guru.
One should not wash his feet.
One should not eat what has been left over.
In this manner, one should acquire one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas.
Then the Vedāṅgas.
But he who, having not studied the Vedas, exerts himself elsewhere, along with his progeny, attains the state of a Śūdra.
Birth from the mother is the first; the second is the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
In this regard, Sāvitrī is his mother, while the teacher is his father.
By this very fact, their status as the twice-born is established.
Before the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, a twice-born man is equal to a Śūdra.
A celibate student should be either shaven-headed or wear matted hair.
After completing the acquisition of the Vedas, having been permitted by his teacher and having given him a gift, he should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna).
Then, he should spend the remainder of his life in the teacher's family alone.
In that regard, when the teacher has passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher himself, or toward the teacher’s wives of equal caste.
In the absence of that, he should become a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī) intent on serving the sacred fire.
The Brahmin who thus practices the life of celibacy without sloth goes to the highest station and is not born here again.
Those who know the Dharma say that for a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), this constitutes a transgression of his vow.
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey, he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them, eating only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year.
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
If one has not gone out for alms and has not kindled the sacred fire, though being free from illness, one shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition, or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.
But one who, having initiated him and performed the instruction in the vows, should teach him the Veda—one should know him as an *ācārya*.
One should know that he who performs another's sacrificial rites is the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
One should not apply anything that has not been examined.
One should not teach [the Veda].
One should not initiate him.

He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two dies or incurs enmity. Where neither dharma nor artha is present, nor even a corresponding desire to listen, there knowledge should not be spoken, just as a good seed is not sown in barren soil.

Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure. Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to one who is unrestrained; in that way, I shall remain potent."
O Brahmin, speak me to that guardian of the treasure who would not deceive you and who would say nothing against you.
Having performed the ritual commencement of the Vedic meters on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, he shall study for four and a half months.
Then he should perform their dismissal outside.
Between the Utsarjana and Upākarma rites, one should study the Vedāṅgas.
One should not study for a day and night on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
Nor during the period of impurity caused by the commencement of another season.
Not during Indra’s departure.
And it does not blow in a fierce wind.
Nor [should one study] during unseasonable rain, lightning, or thunder.
Nor during earthquakes, the falling of meteors, or conflagrations of the quarters.
Nor in a village containing a corpse.
Nor when there is a clash of weapons.
Nor when there is the barking of dogs, the howling of jackals, or the braying of donkeys.
Nor in the sound of musical instruments.
Nor in the vicinity of a Śūdra or an outcaste.
Nor in temples, cemeteries, crossroads, or on main roads.
Nor within the water.
Nor with his feet placed upon a footstool.
Nor on vehicles drawn by elephants, horses, camels, boats, or oxen.
Nor has he vomited it up.
He has not been purged.
One who has indigestion [should not do so].
Nor [is there an offense] in sexual intercourse with those who have not yet reached their fifth year.
Nor during a calamity involving the king, a Vedic scholar, a cow, or a Brahmin.
Nor at the Upākarma ceremony.
Not in emission.
One should not go to sleep after having studied during the latter part of the night.
Even if one is diligent, one should avoid studying during the periods when study is forbidden.
For that which is studied during a period of suspension from study yields no fruit either in this world or the next.
By the study of that [text], there is a depletion of the lifespan of both the teacher and the pupil.
Therefore, one who desires the world of Brahmā should sow knowledge in the field of worthy disciples by means of a teacher, except during the periods of suspension of study.
At the beginning and at the conclusion of the recitation of the Veda, the pupil must perform the clasping of the teacher's feet.
And the Praṇava should be uttered.
And in that regard, by whatever Ṛg verses he recites, by those his ancestors obtain satisfaction through clarified butter.
That which is the Yajus verses, by that honey.
That which is the Sāmans, by that it is milk.
With that which belongs to the Atharvans, [he offers] with the flesh.
By that [study] through which one studies the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Vedāṅgas, and Dharmaśāstras, his food [is rendered pure].

And he who, having acquired knowledge, should live by it in this world—that knowledge shall not yield fruit for him in the next world; as also he who destroys the reputation of others by means of his learning.
And one should not acquire knowledge from another who is studying, unless he has been permitted to do so.
The taking of that [Veda] by him constitutes theft of the Brahman, leading to hell.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should never harbor malice toward the person from whom that knowledge is received.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
one should know that his true birth is that which occurs here from the womb.
But that birth which the preceptor, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule with the Sāvitrī mantra—that is real, and it is free from old age and death.

He who fills one's ears with that which is not false, causing no suffering and bestowing immortality—him one should regard as both father and mother; knowing what he has done for one, one should never bear him ill will.
There are three things that are exceedingly heavy for a person.
The mother, the father, and the teacher.
One must always be intent on serving them.
Whatever they may tell you, that you should do.
One should act for their benefit and welfare.
Without being permitted by them, one should not do anything at all.
These indeed are the three Vedas; these indeed are the three gods; these indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three fires.
The father is the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya.
All duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless.
By devotion to one's mother, one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world; but by service to one's teacher alone, one fully attains the world of Brahmā.

A king, a sacrificial priest, a learned brahmin, one who prohibits unrighteousness, a teacher, a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, an elder brother, and a relative are to be treated like a preceptor.
Their wives should be of the same caste as themselves.
A mother’s sister, a father’s sister, and an elder sister.
For a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, or a priest who is younger than oneself, rising to meet them is itself the salutation.
For wives of teachers who are of lower caste, one should perform a salutation from a distance, but not the touching of their feet.
One should not perform for the wives of one's gurus such acts as rubbing their limbs, applying collyrium, dressing their hair, or washing their feet.
Even if she is a stranger, the wife of another should be addressed as "sister," or as "daughter," or as "mother."
And one should not address one's teachers by the pronoun "you."
If he transgresses that, he should remain without food and, having propitiated him at the end of the day, eat.
And one should not engage in contentious speech with the teacher.
And he should not speak ill of him.
And it is not unintended.
A young wife of one's guru, however, should not be saluted by touching her feet here by a man who has reached his twentieth year and understands virtues and faults.
However, on this earth, a young man should duly perform a salutation to the wives of his gurus who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wife every day and offer salutations, remembering the dharma of the virtuous.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is more weighty than the preceding.
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet, of the two, the Brahmin is the father.
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas by valor,
that of Vaiśyas by grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone by birth.
Now, for a person, there exist three most terrible enemies known as desire, anger, and greed.
This applies especially to householders because of their attachment to possessions.
Therefore, being overcome by this, one engages in minor transgressions, great transgressions, secondary transgressions, and subsidiary transgressions.
In those acts that cause loss of caste, those that cause mixture of castes, and those that render one unworthy of receiving gifts.
And in miscellaneous cases that bring about impurity.
This threefold gateway to hell, which leads to one's own ruin—namely, lust, anger, and greed—one should therefore conquer this triad.
Sexual intercourse with one's mother, sexual intercourse with one's daughter, and sexual intercourse with one's daughter-in-law are crimes of extreme transgression.
But those who have committed heinous crimes should enter the fire;
for indeed, no other means of expiation exists for them in any way whatsoever.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and violating the teacher's wife—these are the great sins (mahāpātakas).
And their conjunction as well.
By associating with one who has fallen from his status for a year, one falls as well.
By means of eating, consuming, and reclining together on the single vehicle.
But through connections such as those of sexual intercourse, the *sruva* ladle, or the principal [offering], impurity occurs immediately.
Those who have committed great sins may be purified by the horse sacrifice, as well as by visiting all the sacred fords on earth.

The killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, of a woman in her menses, of a pregnant woman, of a woman of the Atri lineage, of an embryo whose sex is unknown, and of one who has sought refuge—these are equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa;
while giving false testimony and the killing of a friend are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The seizure of land belonging to a Brāhmaṇa and the misappropriation of a deposit are equal to the theft of gold.
Sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, or a father-in-law, as well as with the wife of a king, is equal to violating the bed of one's guru.
And approaching a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, or a sister [is a cause for loss of caste].
And sexual intercourse with the wives of a learned priest, a sacrificial officiant, a teacher, or a friend.

[Sexual intercourse with] one's sister, a female friend, a girl of the same lineage, a girl of the highest caste, a woman born of the lowest castes (antyajā), a menstruating woman, one who has sought refuge, a female ascetic, and one who has been entrusted [to another].
But these secondary sinners, like the great sinners, are purified by the horse sacrifice or by visiting sacred fords.
Slander that reaches the king.
And the persistent insistence on falsehood toward one's teacher.
Censure of the Vedas.
And [this applies] to the fire, the ancestors, the mother, the son, and the wife.
Eating food that should not be eaten and consuming what is forbidden as food.
The taking away of another's property.
Approaching another man's wife.
Living by improper occupations.
And the acceptance of improper gifts.
The killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a cow.
The sale of what ought not to be sold.
The state of being superseded by a younger brother [is the fault] of the elder brother.
And for him, there is the giving away of his daughter.
Teaching for a fee.
And the taking [of knowledge] from a hired teacher constitutes the acquisition of study through wages.
Mastery over all modes.
The setting in motion of the great machine.
The harming of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and medicinal herbs.
The livelihood of a woman.
And there is engagement in rites of sorcery and acts of forceful power.
The undertaking of action for one's own sake.
The state of not maintaining the sacred fires.
The failure to perform one's obligations toward the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
The study of false treatises.
Nihilism.
Associating with women who drink intoxicants.
Thus end the minor offenses (upapātakas).
But those men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; likewise, they should perform the Parāka penance or sacrifice with the Gosava rite.
Causing pain to a Brahmin.
The smelling of things that should not be smelled and of intoxicants.
Engaging in sexual intercourse with animals.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a word ending in the masculine [gender].
Thus end the acts that cause loss of caste.
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra; if committed unintentionally, one should perform the Prājāpatya.
The killing of domestic or wild animals is an act that causes social intermixture.
Having committed an act that causes confusion of castes, one should eat barley-gruel for a month, or else perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance as an expiation.
Accepting gifts from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, living by usury, speaking untruths, and serving Śūdras—these constitute acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa).
Having committed an act that renders one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance, or by the Śītakṛcchra, or again by the Mahāsāṃtapana.
The killing of birds, aquatic creatures, and those born in water.
And [the same applies] to worms and insects.
Eating at the midday meal.
Thus end the [topics] that bring about impurity.
Alternatively, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance is a means of purification.
That which has not been mentioned is the miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka).
The wise man should perform the expiation as authorized by the Brahmins.
Now, the hells.
Tāmisra.
Andhatāmisra.
Raurava.
Mahāraurava.
The Kālasūtra [hell].
The Great Hell.
The Reviving [Mantra].
The heating.
The Saṃpratāpana [Hell].
The *saṃghāṭaka*.
The *Kākolīya*.
A bud.
Pūtimṛttika.
An iron spike.
The pit.
A perilous path.
The thorny silk-cotton tree.
The river of illumination.
The Forest of Sword-Leaves.
"A prison of iron."
Those who have committed these heinous crimes and have not performed expiation are cooked in turn for an eon.
Those who have committed a mortal sin [remain so] for the duration of a Manvantara.
And those who have committed secondary sins (anupātakin).
For one who has committed a minor offense (upapātakin), it lasts for four yugas.
And those who have committed acts that cause the mixture of castes [must remain so] for a thousand years.
And those who have committed acts that cause the loss of their caste.
And those who have been rendered unworthy of receiving gifts.
And those who have committed acts of defilement.
And for many series of years, those who have committed miscellaneous sins.
Sinful evildoers who have committed transgressions, immediately after giving up their lives, reach the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering.
Just as they are dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama, being led away with great difficulty and groaning.
They are being devoured by dogs, jackals, carnivorous beasts, crows, herons, cranes, and the like, as well as by fire-mouthed creatures, serpents, and scorpions.
They are being burned by fire, pierced by thorns, split apart by saws, and tormented by thirst.
Tormented by hunger and likewise by packs of fierce tigers, they fainted at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
Desiring the food and drink of others, they are beaten by servants with faces as terrifying as those of crows, herons, cranes, and other such birds.
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places they are beaten with pestles; and likewise in some places they are crushed upon iron slabs and stones.
In some places they eat what has been vomited; in some places pus and blood; in some places excrement, and in others flesh that is foul-smelling with the stench of pus—most dreadful.
They remain in dreadful darkness, and in some places they are being devoured by worms with most terrible fire-like mouths.
Then, in some places, most dreadful pretas devour one another.
In some places they are beaten by spirits, and likewise in others they hang suspended;

in some places they are struck by showers of arrows, and in others they are flayed. With their feet placed upon their throats and entwined by the coils of serpents, their backs, heads, and necks are broken; these needle-necked beings are most dreadful.

With bodies the size of gabled palaces, capable of enduring torment, the sinners thus experience their evil deeds and become deeply distressed. Then, for those of sinful nature who have experienced suffering in the hells, there arise births in the animal realm.
For those who commit heinous crimes, there is a succession through all the stationary wombs.
And those who have committed great sins enter the wombs of worms.
Those who commit minor offenses are born into the wombs of birds.
Those who have committed acts that cause the loss of their caste are born into the wombs of aquatic creatures.
Those who have performed acts that cause the mixing of castes are born from the wombs of beasts of prey.
Those who have performed the act of making themselves unworthy of receiving alms are reborn in animal wombs.
For those among humans who have performed defiling actions, there are births in untouchable wombs.
For among those scattered about, they become scattered predators that devour raw flesh.
One who eats the food of those whose food should not be eaten or consumes what should not be eaten becomes a worm.
The thief is the hawk.
The mouse is a stealer of grain.
A swan that steals bell-metal.
He is the heart of the waters; he is the flood of the waters.
The bee is the giver of honey.
The crow drinks milk.
The dog [sees] the taste.
Ghee is Nakula.
Meat is the vulture.
The water-fowl [takes] the fat.
One who drinks oil is called a *tailapāyika*.
Lavaṇa is cīvivāk.
The crane [subsists on] curd.
By stealing silk, one becomes a partridge.
Dardura [is the author] of the Kṣauma [Sūtra].
The krauñca bird [is the deity] of cotton cloth.
The iguana [seizes] the cow.
Vālguda [is] guḍa.
The musk-rat [smells] odors.
Patraśāka is barhī.
Cooked food is the *sedhā* plant.
A śalyaka insect [feeds on] uncooked grain.
The crane [saw] Agni.
Household goods and utensils.
The tortoise [supports] the elephant.
A tiger [seizes] a horse.
A monkey [eats] the fruit or the flower.
The bear [approached] the woman.
The vehicle is a camel.
The vulture [devours] the animals.

Whatever another's property it may be, having seized it by force, a man incurs guilt; likewise, women who seize it by this same method incur guilt as well. They become the wives of those very creatures [from whom they stole].
For those who have transcended the animal state after suffering the miseries of being overcome by hell, the marks appear among human beings.
One who commits a heinous crime becomes afflicted with leprosy.
A killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with consumption.
A drinker of liquor has black teeth.
A stealer of gold has diseased nails.
One who commits adultery with the wife of a guru becomes afflicted with skin diseases.
The slanderer has a putrid nose.
One with a foul-smelling mouth is a slanderer.
A thief of grain becomes deficient in limbs.
Miśracora was Atiriktāṅga.
But one who steals food will suffer from chronic illness.
One who steals speech becomes mute.
One who steals clothing becomes afflicted with vitiligo.
A stealer of horses becomes lame.
One who reviles gods or brahmins becomes mute.
Lolajihva is Garada.
One who sets fire [to a dwelling] shall become insane.
One who is hostile toward the guru becomes afflicted with epilepsy.
But one who kills a cow becomes blind.
And one who steals a lamp.
And he was one-eyed and an extinguisher of lamps.
A washerman is one who sells cane-work, chowries, and lead.
A seller of one-hoofed animals is a hunter.
A bell-ringer is a thief.
A usurer is a "bee-like" person.
One who eats rich food alone suffers from a wind-tumor (vātagulma).
One who breaks the samaya is indeed bald-headed.
One who has committed the offense of emitting semen while under vows suffers from elephantiasis.
One who destroys the livelihood of others is poor.
One who causes suffering to others will suffer from chronic illness.
Thus, by the distinction of their karma, they are born endowed with [physical] marks; likewise, some are afflicted by diseases, while others are blind, humpbacked, lame, or one-eyed.
Dwarfs, the deaf, the mute, and others who are weak—therefore, one should perform expiation with every possible effort.
Now follow the difficult penances (kṛcchra).
He should not eat for three days.
And every day, he should perform the ritual bath at the three sessions of the day.
Three times he immerses himself in the water for the ritual bath.
One should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times with great devotion.
Standing during the day, he should remain standing.
Sitting at night.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
Thus ends the Aghamarṣaṇa.
One should eat in the evening for three days, in the morning for three days, and eat food obtained unasked for three days;
this is the Prājāpatya penance.
One should drink hot water for three days, hot ghee for three days, and hot milk for three days, and one should not eat for three days; this is the *taptakṛcchra* (hot penance).
The cold *kṛcchra* penance consists of these very same [acts] performed in the cold.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk alone for twenty-one days.
The water-kṛcchra consists of consuming water-gruel for one month.
The Mūlakṛcchra penance consists of subsisting on lotus roots.
The Śrīphala-kṛcchra consists of subsisting on bilva fruits.
Or with lotus seeds.
For one who abstains from food for twelve days, it is a Parāka penance.

One should consume cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass for one day; this is the *sāṃtapana* penance. When these same substances, beginning with cow urine, are practiced daily, it is the *mahāsāṃtapana*.
And the *atisāṃtapana* consists of these [austerities] practiced for three days each.

The *parṇakṛcchra* consists of drinking water boiled with the leaves of each of the following plants individually: *kuśa*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *padma*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vaṭa*, *brāhmī*, and *suvarcalā*.
One should avoid excessive conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts; one should constantly recite purificatory mantras and offer oblations according to one's ability.
Now, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should eat morsels that do not cause distortion.
One should increase those [meals] during the waxing moon and not eat at all on the new moon day;
this is the Cāndrāyaṇa known as "barley-shaped" (yavamadhyama).
That [lunar month] in which the new moon occurs in the middle is called "ant-waisted" (pipīlikāmadhya).
If one eats eight mouthfuls every day for a month, that is the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa.
Eating four mouthfuls each at evening and morning constitutes the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
If one should eat three hundred and sixty morsels in a month in any manner whatsoever, that is the common Cāndrāyaṇa.
O Earth, in ancient times, having observed this vow, the stainless Seven Sages, as well as Brahmā and Rudra, attained the supreme abode.
Now, if one should consider oneself heavy due to actions performed by oneself, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel for one's own sake.
One should not offer oblations into the fire after that.
And there is no offering of oblations here.
One should consecrate with mantras that which is uncooked, that which is being cooked, and that which has been cooked.
While it is being cooked, one should perform the protection ritual.
Like a hawk among vultures, like an axe among the forests, Soma goes over the filter, chanting.
And having poured that boiled [milk-rice] into a vessel, he should eat it.

"Those gods who are born of mind, who delight in mind, who are highly skillful, whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us; may they favor us; obeisance to them; to them, svāhā!"—with these words, he should offer the oblation into himself. Then, having sipped water, he should touch his navel.
"O waters, become bathed and drunk within our bellies as barley;
may they be free from disease, free from consumption, and sinless for us—ye goddesses, immortal, increasers of cosmic order."
One who desires intelligence [should do so] for three nights.
One who commits a sinful act [becomes purified] after six nights.
Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself from any one of the great sins (mahāpātakas).
By means of the twelve-night rite, one consumes even the sin committed by one's ancestors.
Having drunk it for a month, all sins [are destroyed].
And for twenty-one nights, [the penance consists of] barley grains as large as cowrie shells.
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey;
you are the cleanser of all sins, a purifier upheld by the seers.
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is indeed the nectar of immortality;
may all of them purify whatever sin or evil deed I have committed.
Whatever deed has been done by speech, whatever deed has been done by action, and whatever evil has been thought by the mind—O barley grains, destroy my misfortune and Kālakarṇī!
And that which has been licked by a dog or a pig, that which is defiled by food-leavings, and the failure to serve one's mother and father—purify all that with my barley.

The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or a period of impurity, the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral—purify these for me with barley.

Purify for me the barley: the rogue child, unrighteousness, whatever is done at the king's gate, the theft of gold, the state of being an *avrātya*, officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice, and the reviling of Brahmins.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva on the twelfth day.
By means of flowers, incense, unguents, lamps, and food offerings, as well as by the satiation of the fire and the Brahmins.
Having observed this vow for a year, one becomes purified from sins.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, one attains Śvetadvīpa.
By observing the twelfth days of both fortnights in this manner for one year, one attains the heavenly world.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, [one attains] the world of Viṣṇu.
In the same way, this also applies to the fifteenth days.
By attending upon Keśava, who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day, and who has become Yoga itself, one shall attain the Great.
In that year, the full moon day on which the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky is declared to be the "Great Full Moon" (Mahatī Paurṇamāsī).

On that day, acts such as giving gifts and observing fasts are proclaimed to be inexhaustible; likewise so is the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight when it is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism.
Having constructed a leaf-hut in the forest, he should dwell there.
One should bathe at the three sessions of the day.
And proclaiming his own deed, he should practice begging for alms from village to village.
And he should sleep on grass.
This is the great vow.
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform [the penance] for twelve years; likewise for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice.
Or one who is pregnant or menstruating.
Or a woman of the Atri lineage.
Or a friend.
In the case of killing a king, one should perform the Mahāvrata penance twice over.
In the case of killing a Kṣatriya, it is three-quarters [of that].
In the case of killing a Vaiśya, the penance is half [of that].
Half of that [penance] is for the killing of a Śūdra.
Having shaved his head, he should follow cows for one month.
While they are seated, he should sit.
And when they are standing, he should remain standing.
And he should rescue those who are sinking.
And one should protect [them] from fears.
Without having provided protection for them from cold and other such afflictions, one should not do so for oneself.
One should bathe with cow urine.
And he should subsist on cow's milk products.
One should perform this cow-vow in the event of killing a cow.
Having killed an elephant, one should give five blue bulls; for a horse, a garment.
For killing a donkey, one [should give] a one-year-old ox.
And in the case of killing a ram or a goat.
For the killing of a camel, the fine is one *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala*.
Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights.
Having killed any one of a mouse, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a water-snake, or a python, and having fasted, he should feed a Brāhmaṇa kṛsara and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee.
For killing a jackal, an owl, a crow, or a fish, one should fast for three nights.
Having killed any one of these—a swan, a crane, a balākā crane, a water-fowl, a monkey, a hawk, a vulture, or a ruddy goose—one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a snake, one should give a black-iron hoe as a gift.
Having killed a eunuch, one [receives] a load of straw.
Having killed a boar, one obtains a jar of clarified butter.
A partridge for one *droṇa* of sesame seeds.
A parrot two years old, like a calf.
A three-year-old Krauñca bird.
For killing a carnivorous beast, one should give a milch cow.
For killing a non-carnivorous wild animal, [the penance is] a heifer.
If one kills an animal unintentionally, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon killing a bird, one should eat only at night.
Or he may give a silver māṣa.
Having killed an aquatic creature, one should observe a fast.
But for the killing of a thousand boneless beings, or for filling a cart [with them], one should perform the vow prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra.
For killing vertebrate animals, one should give something to a Brahmin;
for injuring those without bones, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited; likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
And for those arising from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the purification.
For the unauthorized plucking of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest, one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on a milk-vow.

A drinker of *surā*, excluded from all religious rites, shall subsist on grain-particles for one year; and upon consuming any other kind of intoxicant or impurity, he shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
And [the same penance applies] to eating garlic, onions, leeks, things having a similar odor, village pigs, village cocks, monkeys, or beef.
In all these cases, at the conclusion of the penance, one should perform the sacramental rite again for the twice-born.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows are to be avoided during the rite of re-consecration.
For eating the meat of five-toed animals, with the exception of the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one should fast for seven nights.

Having eaten the food of a member of a religious guild, a courtesan, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights; the same applies to the food of a carpenter and a leather-worker.
And [the water] of usurers, misers, those initiated for a sacrifice, those bound in fetters, those accused of crimes, and eunuchs [is forbidden].
And [the same applies] for those who eat the leftovers of unchaste women, hypocrites, physicians, hunters, cruel people, and fierce people.
And [the impurity lasts for one day] in the case of a woman whose husband is not living, a goldsmith, a rival wife, and those who have fallen from their caste.
And for those who speak slander and untruth, those who have violated their dharma, and those who sell their own bodies or their essence.
And [the same applies] to actors, weavers, ungrateful persons, and washermen.
And [the same applies] to those who perform manual labor, those who sit in wait (such as spies), those who enter the arena (for combat or performance), lute-players, and sellers of weapons.
And [the same applies] for those who live by dogs, for vintners, oil-pressers, weavers, and washermen.
And [the same applies] to those who enter the house of a woman in her menses or of one who has recently given birth.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow [is unfit for consumption].
Touched intentionally with the foot, or sneezed upon.
And [the speech] of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted.
Meat that has not been honored and meat obtained for no purpose.
One who eats the flesh of any fish except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohitaka*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* should fast for three nights.
Having drunk water that has been kept in a vessel for liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights.
And those situated in a vessel for liquor [become pure] after five nights.
Having smelled the scent of one who has drunk liquor, a drinker of Soma shall immerse himself in water, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and then perform the consumption of clarified butter.
For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And having eaten unknown meat from a slaughterhouse or dried meat.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous beasts or birds, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
One should fast for three nights after eating the flesh of the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, haṃsa, rajjudāla, sārasa, dātyūha, śuka, sārikā, baka, balākā, kokila, or khañjarīṭa birds.

For eating the flesh of any bird except for the partridge, the francolin, the quail, the bustard, and the peacock, one must fast for a day and a night. For eating insects, one must drink *brahmasuvarcalā* for one day.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of dogs.
For eating mushrooms or fungi, one must perform the Sāntapana penance.
Having avoided preparations of barley, wheat, and milk, as well as fatty substances, fermented liquids, and *khāṇḍava*, one should consume whatever has been kept overnight and then fast.
And [the juices] of trees produced from incisions or from impure substances, as well as red exudations from trees.
Lotus roots, rice cooked with sesame, kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, fried cakes, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations—these should not be eaten.
And all milks, with the exception of those from cows, goats, and buffaloes.
And those [days] as well, if they are within ten days [of birth].
And those who eat impure food; and those who eat sour substances exclusively, with the exception of curd.
A student in the stage of celibacy (brahmacārin) who eats at a funeral feast (śrāddha) shall fast for three nights.
And he should dwell in water for one day.
For eating honey or meat, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If one eats the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.
If one eats the leavings of another on the following day, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For eating the excrement or urine of five-toed animals, the penance lasts for seven nights.
If one eats at a funeral rite for a living relative (āmaśrāddha), one should subsist on milk for three nights.
A Brahmin who eats the leavings of a Śūdra must observe this for seven nights.
For eating the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal, one must observe a fast for five nights.
For eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, one shall observe a fast for three nights.
But for eating the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa's meal, the penance lasts for one day.
A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra [must fast] for five nights.
One who eats the leavings of a Vaiśya shall fast for three nights.
A Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra; and...
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights.
Having eaten food from a *siddha*, one must perform the *parāka* penance.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated by mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated by mantras.
For as many hairs as there are on the bodies of the animals, so many times has one committed murder here;
yet the Self-born One himself created animals for the sake of sacrifice.
For sacrifice leads to the prosperity of all; therefore, killing in sacrifice is not killing.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain.
Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds, having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states once again.
In the honey-mixture offering, in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods—it is only in these instances that animals may be slain, and never under any other circumstances.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, by killing animals for the sake of sacrifice, leads both himself and those animals to the highest state.

Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. For that violence which is ordained by the Veda and prescribed for this world of moving and unmoving beings—one should know that to be non-violence itself; indeed, Dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead.
He who does not desire to inflict bondage, death, or affliction upon living beings, and who seeks the welfare of all, enjoys ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one performs, and wherever one fixes one's delight—that very thing one obtains without effort, provided one does not harm anything whatsoever.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should avoid meat.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all meat.
He who does not eat meat, even though it be according to custom, like a *piśāca*, becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it—all these are killers.
There is no doer of more demerit than he who, without having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by eating divine fruits and roots, nor by meals of the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He shall devour me in the next world, whose flesh I eat here"—the wise declare this to be the true nature of "flesh" (māṃsa).
One who has committed the theft of gold, confessing his deed to the king, shall offer a wooden pestle.
Through either killing or abandoning [the object], one becomes purified.
Or one should perform the Great Vow for twelve years.
And one who misappropriates a deposit.
One who steals grain or wealth shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year; likewise for the theft of a human being, a woman, a well, a field, or a pond, one shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
The *sāṃtapana* penance is for substances of little value.
For edible foods, drinks, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, and fruits, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For stealing grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses, clothing, leather, or meat, one shall fast for three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one should eat grains for twelve days.
For stealing cotton, silk, wool, and so forth, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon stealing animals with cloven hooves or solid-hooved animals, one should fast for two nights.
For stealing birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or articles made of split bamboo, one should fast for a day.
Whatever a man who is unrestrained might take from others, by that very thing he shall be deprived when he is born again in whatever state of existence.
Since both life and the desire for the Dharma are established upon wealth, one should therefore avoid harming wealth with every possible effort.
He who is intent on harming living beings and likewise he who is intent on harming wealth—of these two, the one intent on harming wealth attains the greater suffering.

Now, regarding approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should dwell in the forest for a year wearing bark garments and perform the Prājāpatya penance according to the procedure for the Great Vow (mahāvrata).
And in the case of going to another's wife.
And for sexual intercourse with a cow, one must observe the cow-vow.
In the case of a man having intercourse with a non-woman, in space, in water, by day, or while riding in a vehicle, one should perform a bath along with one's clothes.
By having sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman, one attains equality with her.
And if it is done through ignorance, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
And for approaching a female animal or a prostitute, one shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a woman who has once been unfaithful to her husband should perform that same vow which is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night, he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting prayers for three years.
Whosoever is of sinful nature, with whomsoever he associates, he shall perform the same expiation as that person.
Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-toed animal or from one that is utterly defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
A member of the royal caste [should wait] for two days.
For one day, he is indeed a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra [should eat] at night.
And at the conclusion of the vow, everyone should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Śūdra drinks the five products of the cow, and a Brāhmaṇa drinks liquor, both of them go to the hell known as Mahāraurava.
If he approaches his wife during her season except on the forbidden days, he shall fast for three nights.
A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brahmin.
If one voids urine or feces in a place lacking water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One who has been released after the sun has risen should bathe with his clothes on and repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one is bitten by a dog, jackal, village pig, donkey, monkey, crow, or an unchaste woman, one should go to a river and perform sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of Brahmins—these shall subsist for one year on alms.

The elder brother who is superseded, the younger brother who supersedes him, the woman through whom he is superseded, the giver [of the bride], and the officiating priest—all these shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells living beings, land, merit, or Soma shall perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.

One who sells fresh medicinal herbs, fragrant substances, flowers, fruits, roots, hides, cane, split bamboo, chaff, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, milk products, oil-cakes, or sesame oil shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
One who sells phlegm, lac, beeswax, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, tin, lead, black iron, udumbara wood, or swords and vessels shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells dyed red cloth, gems, perfumes, molasses, honey, or wool shall fast for three nights.
One who sells meat, salt, lac, or milk shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And one should further bring him close to it.
Having traveled by camel or donkey, or having bathed naked, slept, or eaten, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind, and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing, having performed funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes these sins by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule, one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and been cast out from the status of Brahmanhood, desire to perform expiation.
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation, they are purified by relinquishing it, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and austerity.
In the event of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas, and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the expiation is fasting.
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra.
One should not have any business with those who have been purified from sin; however, one who knows the Dharma should not hold them in contempt once they have undergone purification.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman—even if they are otherwise pure according to the Dharma.
A child who is less than sixteen years old, or one who is eighty years of age, as well as women and the sick, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
Now, for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been stated,
there are secret penances.

Having reached a flowing river and bathed, one who performs sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with their proper characteristics every day, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) once a day, becomes purified from the murder of a Brahmin within a month.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
By means of the vow and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, one who has drunk liquor becomes purified.
By reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one who has committed the theft of gold [is purified].
One who has violated the Guru’s bed is purified by fasting for three nights and performing the recitation and fire-offerings of the Puruṣasūkta.
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, removes all sins, so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins.
A twice-born man should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
indeed, all the sins of the twice-born are consumed by breath control.
One should recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.
A Brahmin who knows the Vedas, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times, a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
A person of the Brahmin, Kshatriya, or Vaishya caste incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, together with the three-footed *Gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness becomes like the wind and, assuming the form of space, attains the supreme Brahman.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth is distinguished as superior to silence.
All Vedic acts of offering oblations and performing sacrifices flow away;
however, the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as the Imperishable, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin.
Now, therefore, follow the purifiers of all the Vedas.
By means of whose recitations and burnt offerings the twice-born are purified from their sins.
The Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
That which is made by the gods.
The Śuddhavatī verses.
The Taratsamandīya hymn.
The Kūśmāṇḍī verses.
The Pāvamānī verses.
Durgāsāvitrī.
Those who are free from attachment.
The hymns of praise consisting of word-stanzas.
The vyāhṛtis are equal to them.
The Bhāruṇḍa birds.
The Candra-sāman.
The two *sāmans* are in the *puruṣavrata*.
The *abliṅga* [is the verse].
The hymn of Bṛhaspati.
The Hymn to the Cow.
The Hymn to the Horse.
And the two Sāmans in the hymn to the Moon.
The Śatarudriya.
The Atharvaśiras.
The Trisuparṇa.
The Great Vow.
The Nārāyaṇīya.
And the Puruṣasūkta.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these songs purify living beings; if one so desires, one attains the memory of past births.
Now, those who are to be abandoned:
The Vrātyas.
They have fallen.
Those who are impure for three generations on both the mother's and the father's side [are ineligible].
All of them are indeed unfit to be eaten from and unfit to receive gifts from.
And one should avoid the habit of accepting gifts from those whose gifts are not to be accepted.
Through the acceptance of gifts, the Vedic luster of Brahmins perishes.
He who accepts a gift without understanding the rules for receiving material objects sinks down together with the giver.
And he who, though capable of accepting gifts, refrains from accepting them, attains the world of the givers.
One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection, meat, honey, a bed, a seat, a house, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered.
Prajāpati considered that alms offered spontaneously upon being invited, presented before him without prior solicitation, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, if he treats her with contempt.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the ancestors and the gods,
he may accept gifts from all sources, but he should not satisfy himself with them.

Even regarding these duties, one who is capable of receiving gifts should not accept them from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy. When the elders have passed away, or when living in the house without them, the following among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten: the landlord, a family friend, and the slave, the cowherd, and the barber; as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Now, for one living in the householder stage of life (gṛhāśramin), there are three kinds of wealth (artha).
White, variegated, and black.
By performing funeral rites for the deceased with pure wealth, one attains divinity through that act.
That which is variegated is human.
That which was done by Kṛṣṇa is that state of being an animal.
That which is acquired by one's own labor is "white" for everyone.
And that which is acquired through an operation separated by one [moment] is black.
Inheritance received in succession, a gift of affection, and property acquired together with one's wife—all such wealth is declared to be "white" (pure) for all without distinction.

That which is obtained from one who has rendered assistance is declared to be "mixed" (śabala). That which is acquired through gambling with associates, theft, forgery, violence, or by means of a pretext is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa).
Whatever a person performs with whatever kind of material substance, he obtains a corresponding fruit both in this world and after death.
A householder should perform the *pākayajñas* in the nuptial fire.
And he performs the Agnihotra sacrifice both in the evening and in the morning.
One should offer oblations to the deities.
One should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa offerings at the times of the conjunction and the opposition of the moon and the sun.
And in autumn and summer, [one should sacrifice] with the Āgrayaṇa.
Or when rice and barley have been cooked.
We have more than a three-year supply.
Every year, with the Soma sacrifice.
In the absence of wealth, [one should perform] the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice.
One should bestow in its entirety all the wealth obtained by begging for the sake of a sacrifice.
One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation both in the evening and in the morning.
And one should give alms to the monk.
By giving alms to one who has been honored, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
In the absence of a monk, one should give even a single mouthful of food to cows.
Or one should cast it into the fire.
Even when food is already being eaten, one should not turn away a beggar.
The mortar and pestle, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water jar, and the broom—these are the five slaughter-houses of the householder.
And for the sake of expiating that, one should perform sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the spirits, the ancestors, and humans.
The private recitation of the Veda is the sacrifice to Brahman.
Man is divine.
The libation to the ancestors is the ancestral rite.
Bali is a ghost.
The sacrifice to men consists of honoring guests.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five—the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts; therefore, the one in the stage of the householder is the best.
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, all place their hopes upon householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.

By constantly practicing the pursuit of the three aims of life, giving food, worshipping the gods, honoring Brahmins, engaging in the study of the Vedas, and performing libations for the ancestors, a householder attains the station of Śakra.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should perform the evacuation of urine and feces.
At night one should face south, during the day one should face north, and at the two twilights one should face east.
Nor on ground that has not been covered.
Nor on ground ploughed by a plow.
Nor in the shade.
Nor on saline soil.
Nor on grassy ground.
Not with a sentient being.
Not in a pit.
Not on an anthill.
Not on a path.
Not on a street.
Nor on another person's impurity.
Not in a garden.
Not on ashes; not on embers.
Not on cow dung.
Not in a cow-pen.
Not in space.
Not in water.
One should not [sit] facing the wind, fire, the moon, the sun, a woman, a teacher, or a Brahmin.
Nor with his head uncovered.
Having rubbed his anus with clods of earth or bricks and holding his penis, he should rise and perform purification with water and earth drawn from the ground, which removes both odor and residue.
One application of earth should be made to the penis, three to the anus, and likewise ten to one hand; seven should be applied to both hands, and three to the two feet.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Now, one should not use a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood.
Nor indeed [should one drink] that which is produced from the Śleṣmātaka, Ariṣṭa, Vibhītaka, Dhava, or Dhanvana trees.
Nor [should one use] that which is produced from the Bandhūka, Nirguṇḍī, Śigru, Tilva, or Tinduka trees.
Nor [should one use] that which is produced from the *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, *pippala*, *iṅguda*, or *guggulu* trees.
Nor [should one use] that which is produced from *pāribhadraka*, *āmlīkā*, *mocaka*, *śālmali*, or hemp.
It is not sweet.
Not sour.
Dried upwards.
It is not hollow.
It is not foul-smelling.
Nor is it slippery.
Nor facing south or west.
And he should eat facing either the north or the east.

Any one of these: the banyan, the *āsana*, the *arka*, the *khadira*, the *karañja*, the *badara*, the *sarja*, the *nimba*, the *arimeda*, the *apāmārga*, the *mālatī*, the *kakubha*, or the *bilva*.
Astringent, bitter, and pungent.

Having its thickness equal to the tip of the little finger, provided with a brush, and twelve finger-breadths in length, one should, having arisen in the morning and restrained speech, consume the tooth-stick.
Having washed and broken it, one should carefully discard it in a clean place;
furthermore, one should never eat a tooth-stick on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
Now, at the base of the pupils of the twice-born, there is the sacred site named Prājāpatya.
At the base of the thumb is the Brahma-tīrtha.
The divine [sacrifice] is performed at the tip of the finger.
At the base of the index finger is that which belongs to the ancestors.

Seated in a clean place, with his knees enclosed and facing either the east or the north, with a focused and cheerful mind, he should sip water that is not hot from fire, free of froth, not offered by a single hand of a Śūdra, and not alkaline;
he should sip three times using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
One should wipe it twice.
One should touch the cavities, the head, and the heart with water.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; women and Śūdras are purified when the water merely touches the lips once.
Then, for the sake of security and well-being, one should approach the Lord.
One should not set out on a journey alone.
Not together with those who are unrighteous.
Nor with Śūdras.
Not by enemies; nor at too early an hour.
Not too late.
Not during the two twilights.
Not at midday.
There is no water kept nearby.
Not too quickly.
Nor should one constantly travel with vehicles drawn by fools, the sick, or those who are afflicted.
Nor with those who lack limbs.
Not with those who are dejected.
Not by means of cows.
Not with those who have not subdued their senses.
Without first giving fodder and water to his draft animals, one should not satisfy one's own hunger and thirst.
One should not stand at a crossroads.
