Nor at the foot of a tree during the night.
Nor an empty dwelling.
Not even a blade of grass.
Nor a prison for cattle.
Nor [should one look at] hair, chaff, potsherds, bones, ashes, or charcoal.
Not cotton seeds.
One should circumambulate the crossroads.
And the worship of the deities.
And the well-known trees.
And [he sees] fire, a brahmin, a courtesan, a full water-jar, a mirror, an umbrella, a banner, a flag, a śrīvṛkṣa tree, a vardhamāna, and a nandyāvarta.
And [the sight of] palm-leaf fans, yak-tail whisks, horses, elephants, goats, cows, curd, milk, honey, and white mustard seeds.
And [the following items]: a lute, sandalwood, weapons, wet cow dung, fruits, flowers, wet vegetables, gorocana, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
And he gave them gifts such as turbans, ornaments, jewels, gold, silver, garments, seats, and vehicles.
Now, having seen those who are intoxicated, insane, or deformed, he should turn back.
And those who have vomited, purged, have shaven heads, wear matted hair, or are dwarfs.
And those who have gone forth as monastics wearing soiled saffron robes.
And [he should provide] fuel consisting of oil, molasses, dried cow dung, grass, palāśa leaves, ashes, and charcoal.
And those who are salt-makers, eunuchs, distillers of liquor, hermaphrodites, cotton-growers, rope-makers, those bound in fetters, and those with disheveled hair.
At the time of departure, one should cause a lute, sandalwood, fresh vegetables, a turban, ornaments, and a young maiden to be greeted with joy.
One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a Brāhmaṇa, a teacher, a tawny cow, or one who has undergone initiation.
And [the water used for] bathing with spittle, vomit, blood, feces, or urine.
One should not step over a calf’s tethering rope.
One should not run while it is raining; one should not cross a river in vain.
Nor [should one eat] without having offered water to the deities and the ancestors.
Not with the two arms.
Not with a broken boat.
One should not stand upon a riverbank.
One should not look into a well.
One should not leap over it.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath (snātaka), women, the sick, ascetics, and those possessing a wheel; however, among these, the king is to be honored, and the snātaka is to be honored by the king.
One should not perform a ritual bath at the water reservoirs of others.
In times of distress, one may perform the rite by taking five lumps of earth and using water instead.
Not when there is indigestion.
Not naked.
Not at night.
Not during the two twilights.
One who is habituated to the morning bath should bathe upon seeing the eastern quarter, copper-red with the dawn.
Having bathed, one should not shake one's head.
One should not draw up water from its source.
One should not touch it as if it were oil.
One should not wear a garment previously worn that has not been washed.
Having bathed, he should wear a turban and two washed garments.
One should not engage in conversation with barbarians, outcastes, or those who have fallen from their caste.
One should bathe in springs, natural pools, and lakes.
Water from the ground is more meritorious than that drawn up [from a well], and water from the Gaṅgā is more meritorious than all other kinds.

Having removed impurities with earth and water, one should enter the water, sit down, and consecrate the bathing place (tīrtha) with the three verses beginning with "apo hi ṣṭhā," the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and the verse "idam āpaḥ pravahata.
Then, submerged in the water, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Or [he may recite]: "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
And Drupadā and Sāvitrī.
Or [he may recite] the section beginning with "They harness the mind."
Or the Puruṣasūkta.
Having bathed and still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libation to the gods and ancestors while remaining in the water.
If he has changed his clothes, it is after having crossed over to the riverbank.
Without having performed the libations for the gods and ancestors, one should not wring out the bathing cloth.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, he should touch [the water].
One should offer flowers to Puruṣa verse by verse with the Puruṣasūkta.
And handfuls of water.
At the very beginning, one should perform the libation for the gods by means of the "divine" (daiva) tīrtha.
Immediately after that, [he should offer] to the ancestors with the ancestral rite.
Therein, first, one should perform the libation for those of one's own lineage.
Then, [he should offer] to the relatives and kinsmen.
Then, [he spoke] to his friends.
In this manner, one should be a daily bather.
And having bathed, he should mutter purificatory texts according to his ability.
Especially the Sāvitrī.
And the Puruṣasūkta.
There is nothing superior to these two.
Likewise, regarding purificatory rites, the chanting of mantras, and giving as prescribed by the rules;
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts [are dispelled].

Therefore, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water for purification (ācamana), one should worship the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, either before an image of the deity or on a consecrated spot.

Having given the gift of life with the mantra "The breath of the Aśvins, may those two [be yours]," and having performed the invocation with the anuvāka beginning with "They yoke the mind," he should perform prostration with his knees, hands, and head.
One should present the *arghya* offering with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
With the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," [he offers] water for the feet (pādya).
"May the waters of the desert be auspicious for us"—with these words, [he offers] water for sipping.
"O Waters, carry this away"—with these words, the bathing powder is applied.
"Upon the chariot, upon the axles, upon the vigor of the bull"—with these words, one applies ointments and ornaments.
"With a young man, well-clothed," [he says] regarding the garment.
"Puṣpāvatī" means "possessing flowers."
"You are the yoke; you are the yoker," [he says] regarding the incense.
"Thou art splendor, thou art semen," [with these words] he offers the lamp.
With the verse "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," he offers the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
The food offering is made with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha."
The fly-whisk, the fan, the measure, the umbrella, as well as the vehicle and the seat—all that he should offer to the God with the Sāvitra mantra alone.
Having thus worshipped, one should then recite the Puruṣasūkta; with that very [mantra], one should offer oblations of clarified butter if one desires the eternal state.
One should not perform rites for the gods or ancestors with water taken at night.
One should not offer an ointment that excludes sandalwood, musk, aloeswood, camphor, saffron, and nutmeg.
Nor [should] clothing dyed with indigo.
An ornament made of gems and gold is not a suitable form of adornment for her.
Not having a foul odor.
It is not produced from thorny plants.
One should offer even that which grows on thorns, provided it is white and fragrant.
One should also offer red saffron and lotuses.
One should not use any living being for the purpose of incense.
There is nothing whatsoever for the purpose of a lamp other than ghee or oil.
Nothing that is forbidden to be eaten should be used for the purpose of an offering.
Nor [should one eat] even what is otherwise edible when it has been prepared with the milk of a goat or a buffalo cow.
And the flesh of five-clawed animals, fish, and boars.
Being self-restrained and pure, one should offer everything with a focused mind and a cheerful disposition, free from haste and anger.

Then, having swept around the fire, sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, and poured water around it, he should take the first portion from all sides of the cooked food and offer it as an oblation.
To Vāsudeva, to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, to Puruṣa, to Satya, to Acyuta, to Vāsudeva.
To Varuṇa, to Indra, and to Indra and Agni;
then, with the remainder of the food, he should offer the bali-oblation to the primary and secondary consumers.
To the east of the fire on all sides.
"Your name was Ambā," "your name was Dulā," "your name was Nitantī."
"Her name was Cupuṇīkā"—this applies to all of them.
"Nandini, Subhage, Sumaṅgali, Bhadraṃkarī"—thus he addressed his own cows while circumambulating them from left to right.
To Sthūṇā Dhruvā, to Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī, and to the Vanaspatis.
At the gateway of dharma and adharma, and at the gateway of death.
To Varuṇa in the reservoir.
"To Viṣṇu," [he says] over the mortar.
"To the Maruts," [he says] over the lower grinding stone.
Above, for King Vaiśravaṇa and for the spirits (bhūtas).
"To Indra and to Indra's men," [he offers] in the eastern half.
"To Yama and to the messengers of Yama," [he offers] in the southern half.
"To Varuṇa and to the attendants of Varuṇa," [he offers] in the western half.
"To Soma, to the Soma-men," [he offers] in the northern half.
"To Brahman, to the attendants of Brahman," [he says] in the middle.
Above, for space.
On the sacrificial ground, he offers during the day with the words, "To the beings that roam by day."
"To those who roam by night" refers to the night.

Then, upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, one should perform the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*) for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, as well as for the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, by means of their names and lineages;
and one should offer ointments, flowers, incense, food offerings, and so forth upon the rice balls.
Having placed a water jar nearby, one should cause a benediction to be recited.
One should offer [the remains] on the ground for dogs, crows, and dog-cookers (outcastes).
And one should give alms.
And one should apply the utmost effort in honoring guests.
One should diligently honor a guest who arrives in the evening.
One should not allow a guest to dwell in one's house without having been fed.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes and as the husband is the lord of women, so is the guest the lord of the householder.
By worshipping that, one attains heaven.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, he departs as one whose hospitality has been denied.
For a Brāhmaṇa staying for only a single night is traditionally called a "guest" (atithi);
because he stays for an uncertain duration, he is therefore called a guest.

One should consider a Brahmin guest from another village, as well as a traveling companion, as a guest who has arrived at one's house, whether it be a household with a wife or even one where the sacred fires are maintained.
But if a Kṣatriya has come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may, at will, feed him as well after the Brahmins have finished eating.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at his household as one who possesses the status of a guest, he should feed them along with his servants, practicing benevolence.

Furthermore, he should, together with his wife, feed with affection other guests who have come to the house—such as friends and others—to the best of his ability, providing them with the food prepared for himself.
One should feed these—female residents, a maiden, a sick person, and likewise a pregnant woman—before the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, his own dependents,
the gods, the ancestors, human beings, his servants, and the household deities have been fed, and after he has honored them, the householder should then eat the remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin; for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.
A householder does not attain such worlds through private Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, or asceticism as he does from honoring a guest.
Every evening and morning, one should offer a seat and water to a guest, as well as food according to one's ability, having honored them in accordance with the prescribed rule.
By giving a shelter, as well as a bed, an oil massage for the feet, and a lamp—each as an individual gift—one obtains a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.
One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Having bathed, one may eat when the two [the sun and the moon] have been released.
On the following day, having bathed after the two [suns] have set without having been released, and having seen them...
One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun that occurs while cows or Brahmins are present.
Nor during the king's misfortune.
When one who has gone abroad considers his agnihotra to have been performed, then he may eat.
When he considers the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice to have been performed, even then [he may proceed].
And when one considers that which was performed on a festival day to be a festival [itself].
And one should not eat when there is indigestion.
Not at midnight.
Not at midday.
Not during the two twilights.
Nor with wet clothes.
He should not wear only a single garment.
Nor should one be naked.
Not in water.
Not hunchbacked.
Nor [should one eat] while seated on a separate seat.
Nor while lying down on a bed.
Not while eating separately; not on one's lap.
Not on earth.
Not in the hand.
And where one might add salt, that one should not eat.
One should not revile children.
Not one [of them] ate the delicacy.
Not from which the oil has been extracted.
One should not eat roasted grains during the day.
One should not [eat] anything related to sesame at night.
Nor curd-mixed barley meal.
Nor [should one eat] the kovidāra, vaṭa, pippala, śāṇa, or śāka plants.
Not having given.
Not without having offered oblations.
And his hands and face are not moist.
And one should not take ghee while still having remnants of food on one's mouth.
One should not gaze at the moon, the sun, or the stars.
One should not touch the crown of the head.
One should not recite the Veda.
One should eat facing the east.
Or facing south.
Having honored [them], [he should offer] food.
Cheerful, wearing garlands, and anointed with unguents.
It would not be exhaustive.
Except for curd, honey, ghee, milk, barley-meal, and sweet cakes.
One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor while standing; many should not look on at one person, nor should many eat together in one place.
One should never drink water from one's cupped hands in an empty house, a fire-chamber, or a temple; nor should one eat to complete satiety.

One should not eat a third meal, nor anything unwholesome under any circumstances; one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat again in the morning.
One should not eat food that is defiled by intention, nor from a vessel defiled by intention; nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth around the knees.
One should not approach a woman on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight.
Nor after having eaten at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*).
Not after having given.
He was not invited to the śrāddha feast.
Not in temples, cremation grounds, or empty dwellings.
Nor at the roots of trees.
Not by day.
Not during the two twilights.
It is not defiled.
Nor one who is afflicted by disease.
Nor one who is afflicted by disease.
One who desires to live a long life should not approach a woman who is deficient in limbs, nor one with extra limbs, nor likewise one who is older in years, nor a pregnant woman.
One should not sleep with wet feet.
Neither with the head toward the north nor toward the south.
Not naked.
Not along the backbone.
Not in space.
Nor on a bed made of *pālāśa* wood.
Nor [should one use] that which is made from five kinds of wood.
Not for the purpose of crushing elephants.
Nor for one who has been burned by lightning.
Not in what is divided.
Not on the back of a fire.
Nor is it produced from a tree watered by a jar.
Nor in cremation grounds, empty dwellings, or temples.
Nor among the fickle.
Not in the midst of women.
Nor over grain, cattle, a teacher, fire, or deities.
One should not sleep while impure from food remnants, nor during the day, nor during the two twilights, nor on ashes; nor in an unclean place, nor on moist ground, nor on the summit of a mountain.
Then, one should not despise anyone at all.
And one should not mock those who have missing or extra limbs, nor fools, nor those destitute of wealth.
One should not serve those who are inferior.
One should not perform any action that is obstructive to the private recitation of the Vedas.
One should adopt an appearance appropriate to one's age.
Of learning, noble lineage, wealth, and country.
Not arrogant.
One should constantly examine the scriptures and other such sources.
One should not say "it does not exist. One should not wear garlands that are scentless, pungent, or dyed red.
One should wear even a red lotus.
And a bamboo staff.
And a water-pot containing water.
The sacrificial thread shall be made of cotton.
And two earrings made of gold.
One should not look at the rising sun.
Nor one who is setting.
Nor [should one look at] that which is concealed by a garment.
Nor does it reside in the middle of a mirror or water.
Not at midday.
One should not look at the face of an angry teacher.
Nor should one look at one's own reflection in oil or water.
Not in a mirror covered with dirt.
One should not [look at] one's wife at the time of eating.
Nor a naked woman; nor anyone urinating.
Nor [should one approach] an elephant that has broken loose from its tethering post.
And one situated in an unfavorable position should not engage in a fight with a bull or similar animals.
Not intoxicated.
Not intoxicated.
One should not throw impure substances into the fire.
Nor blood.
It is not poison.
Also in water.
One should not step over fire.
One should not warm one's feet [over a fire].
One should not wipe oneself on *kuśa* grass.
One should not wash it in a bronze vessel.
One should not place one foot upon the other.
One should not draw on the ground.
One should not be a cutter of grass.
One should not cut one's nails or hair with one's teeth.
And he should avoid gambling.
One should not wear garments, sandals, garlands, or sacred threads that have been worn by another.
One should not impart sacred knowledge to a Śūdra.
Nor [should one eat] the remnants of an offering.
Nor sesame seeds.
And one should not teach him the Dharma.
It is not a vow.
One should not scratch the head or the belly with both hands joined together.
One should not refuse curd or jasmine.
One should not pull a garland from oneself.
One should not awaken one who is asleep.
One should not cause one who is attached to become dispassionate.
One should not speak to a woman in her courses.
Nor among the Mlecchas or the lowest castes.
In the presence of the fire, the deity, and the Brāhmaṇas, he should raise his right hand.
One should not point out a cow that is grazing in another's field.
Nor [should one touch] a calf while it is drinking.
One should not cause those who are agitated to rejoice.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra.
Nor in a place crowded with unrighteous people.
One should not dwell with one who is devoid of a physician.
Nor when it is defiled.
Not for long on the mountain.
One should not engage in futile exertion.
Nor [should one engage] in dancing or singing.
Nor should one snap one's fingers.
One should not utter vulgar speech.
Not untruth.
Nor what is unpleasant.
One should not touch anyone at a vital point.
One who desires to live a long life should not despise oneself.
One should perform the twilight worship for a long time.
One should not play with snakes or weapons.
One should not touch the apertures of the body with a state of mind free from signs.
One should not raise a stick against another.
One who is to be disciplined should be struck for the sake of discipline.
One should apply it to the back with a bamboo splinter or a cord.
One should avoid speaking ill of gods, brahmins, the scriptures, and great-souled beings.
And wealth and pleasure that are contrary to the Dharma [should be abandoned].
And even a dharma that is loathed by the world.
And on the festival days, one should perform propitiatory fire-offerings.
One should not cut even a blade of grass.
And he should remain adorned.
In this way, one should be a practitioner of proper conduct.

One obtains long life through right conduct (*ācāra*), and through right conduct one attains the desired goal— that which is righteous (*dharmya*), proclaimed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and practiced by the virtuous.
Even a man who is devoid of all auspicious marks, if he possesses good conduct, is full of faith, and is free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
One should abide in self-restraint.
And the restraint of the senses is proclaimed as *dama*.
This world and the next belong to the self-controlled.
No action whatsoever succeeds for one who has not restrained their speech.
Self-control is the supreme purifier; self-control is the highest auspiciousness.
Through self-control one obtains everything that one desires in the mind.
Travelling in a chariot yoked with five horses, which moves at the speed of thought and follows the noble path—if the horses do not carry that chariot away, then enemies do not defeat the Tathāgata.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
Then, one desiring to perform a śrāddha should invite the Brahmins on the day before.

On the second day, in the forenoon during the bright fortnight or in the afternoon during the dark fortnight, he should cause the Brahmins—who have bathed well and performed the ritual sipping of water—to sit upon seats covered with Kuśa grass, arranged according to their seniority.
Two for the gods facing east, and three for the ancestors facing north.
"Or one by one in both cases."
In the case of *āmaśrāddhas* and those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one should offer oblations into the fire using the first pentad [of verses].
In the Śrāddha rites for animals, [one should perform it] with the middle group of five.
On the new moon days, by means of the excellent group of five.
After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, on the eighth days of the dark fortnights, one should perform [the rites] respectively with the first, middle, and highest sets of five [verses].
And also on the Anvaṣṭakā days.
Then, permitted by the Brahmins, he should invoke the ancestors.
Having performed the dismissal of the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds while reciting the two verses beginning with "apayantu asurāḥ," [he should proceed].

Having performed the invocation with the mantra, "O Pitṛs, may all of them come to me first; this is for you, O Pitṛs," and having offered water for the feet mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds, using the mantras "Those who stand as immortal speech" (*yās tiṣṭhanty amṛtā vāk*) and "That which is mine, O Mother" (*yan me mātā*), and having prepared and presented the *arghya*, applied the unguents, and honored the Brahmins according to his ability with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, garments, flowers, ornaments, incense, and lamps, he should take food soaked in ghee and [offer it] to the Ādityas...
Having looked at them, saying, "O Rudras and Vasus," and having said, "I shall perform [the rite] in the fire," and being told by the Brahmins, "Do so," he should offer three oblations.

Having performed the consecration of the oblation with the mantra, "O my ancestors, this sacrifice is for you, O fathers," he offers it to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, according to their names and lineages, into the fires as they are available, while facing north.
While the Brahmins are eating, one should mutter: "Whatever [fault] of mine [has occurred] through excess during the days and nights, or whatever raw flesh you have consumed."
And the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras.
Near the remnants of the food, upon kuśa grass with its tips pointing southward, he should place one rice-ball for the father, saying: "The earth is an inexhaustible ladle."
"The atmosphere is the imperishable ladle"—with these words, he offers the second pinda to the grandfather.
"May the sky be the inexhaustible ladle"—this is the third [offering] for the great-grandfather.
To those ancestors who have passed away here, a garment should be given with the words, "O ancestors who have departed."
"O Fathers, bestow heroic food upon us"—thus [he offers] the food.

"O ancestors, rejoice here according to your respective portions"—with these words, he rubs his hands at the base of the *darbha* grass. Having scattered water around the *piṇḍas* clockwise with the mantra "Bringing strength," he should present the *arghya*, flowers, incense, ointments, food, and various kinds of eatables and delicacies.
And a water vessel combined with honey, ghee, and sesame seeds.

When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, he should sprinkle the food along with the grass with the words, "May it not be exhausted for me," and having placed the scattered remnants of food before the leavings,

he should then offer [water] while they face the east. Then, having sprinkled the site of the Śrāddha with the words, "Well-sprinkled," he should perform everything while holding Darbha grass in his hand.
Then, having circumambulated from the front while facing east, saying "That which belongs to me, O Rāma," and having returned, he should mutter the mantra: "The gods and the ancestors."

Having offered the inexhaustible water with the [guests'] names and lineages, saying "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should then, facing eastward with palms joined and mind focused on that, request [the blessing] with a joyful heart.
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny; may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
They should say, "So be it."
"May we have abundant food, may we receive guests, may there be those who ask of us, and may we not have to ask anything of anyone"—having thus accepted these blessings with these two verses.

Then, having honored the Brahmins according to the rule, followed them, and saluted them, he should dismiss them with the mantra "vāje vāje. On the Anvaṣṭakās, having performed the Śrāddha preceded by the rites for the gods (daivapūrva) with vegetables, meat, and cakes, and having offered oblations into the fire as on the Aṣṭakās, he should likewise feed the Brahmins—preceded by the rites for the gods—for his mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother; then, after giving sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should dig pits.
At its root, having performed the kindling of the fire toward the east and north, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) takes place.
At the base of the three furrows for men, and at the base of the three furrows for women.
One should fill the three pits for the person with food and water.
For a woman, three furrows [should be sown] with cooked rice and milk.
With curd, meat, and milk, [he should offer] three trenches each.
Having filled [the vessel], one should recite this mantra: "May this be inexhaustible for you, sirs, and for you, ladies."
If one should perform a śrāddha while his father is still living, he should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it.
Those whose father and grandfather are living, while their great-grandfather is also alive.
One should not perform it at all while the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are still living.
He whose father is deceased should, having placed a rice-ball for his father, offer [rice-balls] to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather.
He whose father and grandfather are deceased should, having offered two rice-balls to them, offer one to his grandfather’s grandfather.
He whose paternal grandfather has passed away should, after placing a rice-ball for him, offer two rice-balls beyond the great-grandfather.

A wise person should likewise perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers; he should do so according to the rule by substituting the appropriate mantras, while for the remaining ancestors it is performed without mantras.
The new moon day, the three Aṣṭakās, the three Anvaṣṭakās, the Māghī, the Prauṣṭhapadī, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight thereafter, and the ripening of rice and barley.
One who does not perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) for these [ancestors] falls into hell.
The transit of the sun.
The two equinoxes.
Especially the two solstices.
The Vyatīpāta yoga.
The birth asterism.
Prajāpati has indeed declared these to be the optional times for the śrāddha;
whatever śrāddha is offered on these occasions conduces to infinity.
Indeed, the wise should not perform a *śrāddha* during the two twilights or at night;
for a *śrāddha* offered at the sight of Rāhu lasts as long as the moon and stars.
By constantly performing a *śrāddha* on a Sunday, one attains good health.
And good fortune is found in the lunar mansion of Ārdrā.
Victory in battle [is attained] when Mars is [favorable].
All desires are fulfilled in the state of awakening.
One obtains the desired knowledge in the Jaiva [mantra].
Wealth [is obtained] in the period of Venus.
Life is [determined] by Saturn.
One attains heaven under the asterism Kṛttikā.
Offspring is obtained through the Rohiṇīs.
One who desires spiritual luster should offer it in the north-eastern quarter.
The accomplishment of rites is achieved in the Raudra [mudrā].
One should perform the *bhū* rite under the asterism Punarvasu.
Prosperity under Puṣya.
Prosperity in the serpent [world].
All desires [are fulfilled] at the ancestral rite.
Good fortune is in the lot of fortune.
While acquiring wealth.
Preeminence among kinsmen is in the hand.
The sons of Rūpavatī [are born] from Tvaṣṭṛ.
Success in trade is attained under Svāti.
Gold [is obtained] under the Viśākhā asterism.
Friends are friendly.
Sovereignty [is attained] among the Śakras.
Agriculture [is taught] in the Root [Treatise].
Success in sea voyages is attained in the sign of Scorpio (Āpya).
One obtains all desires through the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Supremacy is attained through victory.
All desires [are fulfilled] through hearing.
Or salt in the dwelling of Vāsava.
In the western quarter there is health; in the southern quarter there is base metal.
The house is in the depths of the waters.
One should give cows in the sacrifice to Pūṣan.
One should worship the horses during the month of Āśvina.
Life is in the south.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), beautiful women come to one's house.
One should worship Kanyā, the giver of boons, on the second lunar day.
All desires [are fulfilled] on the third day.
On the fourth day, [he should sacrifice] animals.
On the fifth day, one obtains handsome sons.
Victory in gambling on the sixth day.
Agriculture on the seventh day.
Trade on the eighth day.
On the ninth day, [he offers] animals.
The *vājina* offerings on the tenth day.
On the eleventh day, one obtains sons endowed with Vedic splendor.
Gold and silver on the twelfth day.
Good fortune [is attained] on the thirteenth day.
All desires [are fulfilled] on the fifteenth day.
For the Śrāddha rite of those killed by weapons, the fourteenth day is prescribed as auspicious.
Furthermore, there are two verses sung by the ancestors:
"May there arise in our family some supreme among men, who, being composed in mind, [attains this] on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight during the rainy season."

He who performs the śrāddha rite with honey-sweetened milk-rice throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or during the time when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east, [attains great merit].
Now, one should not perform a *śrāddha* with water taken at night.
In the absence of kuśa grass, one should place kāśa or dūrvā grass in the place of the kuśa.
For the purpose of clothing, [he may accept] thread made from cotton.
One should discard the fringe, even if it is made of new cloth.
Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, and those produced on thorny plants.
One should offer white, fragrant flowers—even those grown on thorny plants—as well as water-born flowers and red ones.
One should not offer fat or marrow for the purpose of a lamp; rather, one should offer ghee or oil.
One should not offer anything derived from living beings for the purpose of incense.
One should administer guggulu combined with honey and clarified butter.
Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka wood for the purpose of unguents.
One should not give salt that has been seen with one's own eyes.
And with the hand, [one offers] ghee, condiments, and so forth.
One should give vessels made of metal.
Especially those made of silver.
One should place a sword, a mat of grass, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and unbroken grains—items that are purifying and destructive of demons.
And black gram, lentils, stale food, and prepared salt.
One should avoid anger; one should not shed tears.
But one should not act with haste.
For the offering of ghee and other substances, vessels made of precious metals, vessels of khaḍga wood, and vessels of phalgu wood are recommended.
And on this point, there is a verse:
That which is given with a sword made of gold or silver, or of udumbara wood, or even with a vessel of phalgu wood, attains imperishability.
With sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, śyāmāka, priyaṅgu, nīvāra, and mung beans, as well as wheat, they are gratified for a month.
For two months, [one should subsist] on fish meat.
Three with the meat of the spotted antelope.
And four by the thief-cloud.
Five [oblations] with the Śākuna [sāman].
Six [oblations] with a goat.
Seven [times] with the Raurava [Sāman].
Eight with the flesh of the spotted deer.
With a young bull.
Ten [times] by means of buffalo meat.
But eleven [cakes] with a hornless goat.
For one year, he should subsist on cow’s milk or its various derivatives.
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
We shall eat black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the meat of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane, and rhinoceroses—provided they are devoid of horns—as long as the sun endures.
One should not place food upon a seat.
One should not touch it with the feet.
One should not spit upon it.
One should dispel the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds or mustard seeds.
And one should perform the act of faith in seclusion.
One should not look at a woman who is menstruating.
Nor a dog.
Nor a village pig.
Nor a village cock.
One should diligently cause the Śrāddha ceremony for the Unborn One to be performed.
And the Brahmins, restrained in speech, should eat.
Nor for one whose head is wrapped.
Nor with shoes on.
Nor with their feet placed upon a stool.
Those with missing limbs or extra limbs shall not behold the faithful one.
Nor Śūdras.
They have not fallen.
At that time, he should honor a Brahmin or a mendicant with the consent of the Brahmins.
When asked by the giver, the Brahmins should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
As long as there is heat in the food, as long as those who eat remain restrained in speech, so long do the ancestors eat—until the qualities of the sacrificial offering have been described.
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water, he should cast it upon the ground in front of those who have finished eating, scattering it about.
The remnants that have fallen upon the ground at a rite for the ancestors are declared to be the share of the group of servants who are upright and free from deceit.
In rites dedicated to the gods, one should not examine a Brāhmaṇa.
One should examine [the suitability of] a person for rites concerning the ancestors with great care.
One should avoid those with missing or extra limbs.
And those who persist in improper occupations.
Those who follow the "vow of the cat."
Physicians.
The sons of unmarried women.
His sons.
Those who perform many sacrifices.
Those who officiate as priests for an entire village.
Those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
Those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice.
The Vrātyas.
Those who make ornaments for festivals.
Those who teach for a fee.
Those taught by a hired teacher.
Those nourished by the food of Śūdras.
From association with those who have fallen [from their caste].
Those who do not study.
Those who have fallen away from the twilight devotions.
The king's servants.
The naked ones.
Those who are disputing with their father.
And those who abandon their father, mother, teacher, the sacred fire, or their Vedic study.
A wise man should diligently avoid these [persons] during the performance of a śrāddha rite.
Now, those who purify the row.
One who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire.
The one who maintains the five fires.
One who chants the Jyeṣṭha-sāman.
One who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
He who has mastered even a single auxiliary limb of the Vedas.
One who has mastered the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and grammar.
He who has reached the further shore of even a single treatise on Dharma.
Purified by sacred fords.
Purified by sacrifice.
Purified by austerity.
Purified by truth.
Purified by mantra.
He is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
The lineage of the Brahmadēya.
The Trisuparṇa.
Son-in-law.
And especially so for the yogin.
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
May there be such a person in our family who would diligently feed a yogi brahmin at a śrāddha ceremony, by which we ourselves may be satisfied.
One should not perform a *śrāddha* rite in a region inhabited by barbarians (*mleccha*).
One should not go to a land of barbarians.
Having drunk water from another's well, one comes to attain equality with it.
That country in which the established order of the four castes does not exist should be known as a land of Mlecchas; beyond that is Āryāvarta.
Now, at Puṣkara, the śrāddha is inexhaustible.
And recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities.
By merely bathing at Puṣkara, one becomes purified from all sins.
In the same way, it is at Gayāśīrṣa.
At the banyan tree.
On Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
On Mount Varāha.
Anywhere along the banks of the Narmadā.
On the bank of the Yamunā.
Especially in the Gaṅgā.
At Kuśāvarta.
O Binduka!
On Mount Nīla.
At Kanakhala.
In Kubjāmra.
At Bhṛgutuṅga.
In Kedāra.
In the Mahālaya [shrine].
At Naḍantikā.
In Sugandhā.
In Śākambharī.
At Phalgutīrtha.
In the great Gaṅgā.
In the village of Trihalikā.
In Kumāradhārā.
At Prabhāsa.
Anywhere along the Sarasvatī, and especially so.
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, constantly in the Naimiṣa forest, and especially in Vārāṇasī.
In the hermitage of Agastya.
In the hermitage of Kaṇva.
In the Kauśikī [River].
On the bank of the Sarayū.
At the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotiṣā.
At Śrīparvata.
In Kālodaka.
In Uttaramānasa.
In the submarine fire.
At Mataṅgavāpī.
O you who possess the seven seers!
In the footstep of Viṣṇu.
In the steps on the path to heaven.
At the Godāvarī.
In the Gomatī.
In the Vetravatī river.
In the Vipāśā river.
In the Vitastā river.
On the bank of the Śatadrū.
On the Candrabhāgā [River].
In the Irāvatī.
On the bank of the Sindhu.
To the south is Pañcanada.
Auspicious!
And likewise in these and other sacred fords (tīrthas).
In the best of rivers.
In all intrinsic natures as well.
On the sandy banks.
In the springs.
On the mountains.
In the groves.
In the forests.
In the groves.
In houses smeared with cow dung.
Toward those things that are pleasing to the mind.
And in this regard, there are verses sung by the ancestors:
May that being be born in our family who shall offer us handfuls of water in rivers abounding with water, especially those that are cool.
"May there arise in our family some supreme among men who, with a concentrated mind, shall perform for us the śrāddha ceremony at the banyan tree of Gayāśīrṣa."

One should desire many sons, so that even one of them might go to Gayā, or perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull. Now follows the ritual for the release of the bull (vṛṣotsarga).
In that regard, one should first examine the bull.
The son of a milch cow that has a living calf.
Endowed with all the primary marks.
Blue.
Or it is red, with the face, tail, feet, and horns being white.

[He should provide] a cover for the herd. Then, having strewn grass around a well-kindled fire in the midst of the cows, having cooked a *caru* offering for Pūṣan with milk, and having offered it while reciting, "May Pūṣan follow our cows; may there be delight here," he should have an ironworker [fashion] a disc on one side of a bull and a spear on the other side.
And one should bathe [the image] marked [with these signs] with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā" and with the verse "śaṃ no devīḥ."
Having brought him, bathed and adorned, together with four heifers likewise bathed and adorned, one should recite the Rudra-hymns, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.
One should recite "Father of calves" into the right ear of the bull.
And this:
For the Blessed Lord Dharma is proclaimed to be a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion, and may he protect me in every way.

I give this young man to you as a husband; sport and move about with him, your beloved. May we not be deprived of our offspring nor of our bodies; O King Soma, may we not fall into the power of the enemy.
One should cause a bull yoked with a heifer to be placed in the northeastern direction; one should give the officiating priest a pair of garments, as well as gold and bell-metal.
One should provide food with abundant ghee and feed the Brahmins there.
In whatever reservoir of water a bull released for sacrifice drinks, that entire reservoir stands as an offering to his ancestors.
Wherever an elephant, full of pride, scratches the ground with its tusk, there abundant food and drink for the ancestors is provided.

Then, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having prepared a black antelope skin complete with its hooves and horns— its horns adorned with gold, its hooves with silver, and its tail with pearls— one should spread it upon a woolen cloth and then cover it with sesame seeds.
And one should fashion a golden navel.
One should cover it with a pair of unwashed garments.
And one should adorn it with all kinds of perfumes and jewels.

In the four directions, one should visualize four fiery vessels filled with milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter, and give them to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, who is adorned and covered with a pair of garments;
and on this matter, there are these verses:
But he who should give a black antelope skin, complete with hooves and horns, covered with sesame seeds and cloths, and adorned with all kinds of jewels;
By him the earth, including its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves, extending to its four boundaries, would have been given; of this there is no doubt.
He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a brahmin overcomes all evil deeds.
Now, when a cow is giving birth, she becomes the earth.
Having given her, thus adorned, to a brahmin, one obtains the fruit of the gift of the earth.
On this point, there is a verse:
By giving a cow with its calf and its udders intact, one who is faithful and composed attains heaven for as many eons as there are hairs on the bodies of both.
The month of Kārttika has Agni as its presiding deity.
And Agni is the mouth of all the gods.

Therefore, by bathing outdoors during the month of Kārttika, being devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) only once a day, one becomes purified from the sins committed throughout the year.

One who bathes daily throughout the entire month of Kārttika, having conquered the senses, reciting prayers, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and remaining self-controlled, is liberated from all sins.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when it is conjoined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should cause a Brahmin to receive at moonrise one *prastha* of powdered salt with a golden center.
By this karma, one is born endowed with beauty and good fortune.

On that day, having rubbed his body with a paste of white mustard seeds, having been consecrated with a jar filled with cow’s ghee, and having bathed with all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, and all seeds, he should bathe the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva with ghee; having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, and having offered oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava, Śākra, and Bārhaspatya mantras, he should cause the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce auspicious blessings with ghee mixed with gold. He should give a pair of garments to the officiant.
By this action, it is nourished.
If the month of Māgha is joined with the Maghā constellation, by performing a śrāddha with sesame seeds on that day, one becomes purified.
If the Phālgunī [nakṣatra] is conjoined with the day of Phalguna, by offering on that day a well-prepared and well-spread bed to a Brahmin, one obtains a charming wife who is beautiful and wealthy.
Nor does a wife [desire] her husband.
By the gift of variegated garments on that [day], one attains good fortune.

If the Vaiśākhī full moon is conjoined with the Viśākhā nakṣatra, one who gratifies seven Brahmins with sesame seeds mixed with honey on that day, thereby pleasing Dharmarāja, becomes purified from sins.

If the full moon day of Jyaiṣṭha (Jyaiṣṭhī) should coincide with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, by the gift of an umbrella and sandals on that day, one attains lordship over cattle. On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha (Āṣāḍhī) joined with the Āṣāḍhā nakṣatra, by the gift of food and drink, one attains that very same [lordship] in an inexhaustible manner.
By giving a water-cow together with cooked rice, covered with a pair of garments, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa when it is conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā, one attains heaven.
On the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, when it is conjoined with the Proṣṭhapadā asterism, one becomes liberated from all sins by the gift of a cow.
On the full moon day of Āśvayuja, when the moon has entered the asterism Aśvinī, by giving a vessel filled with ghee along with gold to a Brahmin, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire.

In that [constellation], having given a white bull or one of another color, endowed with all grains, jewels, and perfumes, to a Brahmin at the rising of the moon in the middle of a lamp-offering, one does not see the fear of a wilderness.

Having fasted on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one who worships Śrī Vāsudeva with unbroken grains (akṣata), and having offered those same grains as oblations and given them as gifts, becomes purified from all sins.
And whatever one gives on that day attains imperishability.

When the full moon of Pauṣa has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who has fasted, bathed with sesame seeds, offered a libation of sesame, worshipped Vāsudeva with sesame, and likewise offered oblations, given gifts, and eaten, becomes purified from sins.

When the full moon of Māgha has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, having observed a fast and reached the Śravaṇa asterism, one should offer two lamps with two large wicks before the venerable Vāsudeva.
On the right side, having offered a full cloth dyed with safflower and a weight of ghee increased by eight [units].
On the left side, having placed eight [offerings] mixed with sesame oil, together with an entire white cloth.
Having performed this, in whatever kingdom, in whatever region, or in whatever family one is born, one becomes radiant therein.
By giving ghee daily to Brahmins throughout the entire month of Āśvina and thereby pleasing the two Aśvins, one becomes possessed of beauty.
In that very month, by feeding Brahmins daily with products of the cow, one becomes a sharer in the kingdom.

Every month, when the moon is conjoined with the asterism Revatī, one who feeds Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee for the propitiation of Revatī, and thereby gratifies Revatī, becomes a possessor of beauty. In the month of Māgha, by offering oblations of sesame seeds into the fire every day and feeding Brāhmaṇas with boiled grain and ghee, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire.
Having bathed in river water on every fourteenth day and having worshipped Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from all sins.
If one desires vast enjoyments associated with the moon, the sun, and the planets, one should always bathe in the morning during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna.
Then, when water begins to flow from that well dug by the excavator, half of his misdeed is destroyed.
The maker of a pond, being eternally satisfied, attains the world of Varuṇa.
One who gives water is always satisfied.
For one who plants trees, those trees become sons in the next world.
One who gives trees gratifies the gods with the flowers of those trees.
And [he should honor] guests with fruits.
And with shade for those who have arrived.
When the god rains down water, he [satisfies] the ancestors.
One who builds a bridge attains heaven.
One who builds a temple for a deity attains the very world of that deity for whom he constructs the temple.
Having sprinkled it with white plaster, it shines with glory.
Having performed it in various ways, one attains the world of the Gandharvas.
By the offering of flowers, one becomes glorious.
By the gift of ointments, one becomes possessed of fame.
By the gift of a lamp, one becomes possessed of vision and radiant everywhere.
By the gift of food, one becomes strong.
By removing the floral offerings made to the gods, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
By sweeping the temple of a deity, by smearing it with cow dung, by cleaning the remnants of a Brahmin's meal, by washing his feet, and by attending to him when he is unwell.
One who restores wells, groves, ponds, and temples obtains the primary fruit [of the original merit].
The gift of fearlessness is superior to all other gifts.
By giving that, one attains the desired world.
And by the gift of land.
By giving even a piece of land the size of a cow's hide, one becomes purified from all sins.
By the gift of a cow, one attains the heavenly world.
The giver of ten cows [attains] the worlds of cattle.
The giver of a hundred cows [attains] the worlds of Brahmā.

Having given a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, a pearl-adorned tail, a bronze milking vessel, and a cloth as a covering, one attains the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on the cow's body.
Especially a tawny cow.
By giving a tamed bull capable of bearing the yoke, one becomes the donor of ten cows.
The giver of a horse attains the same world as the sun.
By giving clothing, one attains the same world as Candra.
By the gift of gold, one attains residence in the same world as Agni.
Through the gift of form, one obtains form.
By the gift of vessels made of refined gold, one becomes a fit recipient for all desires.
Through the gift of ghee, honey, and oil, one attains health.
By the giving of medicine.
And by the gift of salt, one obtains beauty.
Through the gift of grain, one attains satisfaction.
And by the gift of grain.
The giver of food obtains everything.
Through the gift of grain, one obtains good fortune.
The giver of sesame seeds obtains desired offspring.
And in battle, he attains complete victory.
By the offering of a seat, one gains a place.
By the gift of a bed, one obtains a wife.
By the gift of sandals, one obtains a chariot yoked with mules.
By the gift of an umbrella, one attains heaven.
By the gift of palm-leaf fans and yak-tail whisks, one attains comfort on the journey.
Through the gift of a building site, one attains sovereignty over a city.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is held dear in the home, that very thing should be given to one endowed with virtue by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
What is given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal result in the world beyond.
Twice as much for one who is a Brahmin in name only.
One who has studied [the Veda] thoroughly gains a thousandfold [reward].
To one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas, [the gift] is infinite.
But the domestic priest is the vessel for himself alone.
A sister, a daughter, and a daughter-in-law.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat, nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas.

One who carries the banner of Dharma while being always greedy, deceitful, and a hypocrite in the world; one who acts like a cat, violent, and a deceiver of all—such a person should be known as a "cat-vowed" practitioner (*baiḍālavratika*).
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends, crafty, falsely humble, and devoted to the "heron-vow" (hypocrisy), is so called.
Those in this world who practice the vow of the heron and those who bear the mark of the cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful action.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma; by concealing the sin with a vow, one merely practices deception upon women and *śūdras*.
Such a Brahmin is censured by those who discourse on the Veda both in this world and after death; furthermore, a vow practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas.

One should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor to a benefactor, nor to those whose character is devoted to dancing and singing; it is certain that a gift is given for the sake of Dharma.
Upon seeing the wrinkles and grey hair, a householder should take refuge in the forest.
Or upon seeing the offspring of one's own offspring.
Or, having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may go followed by her.
There too, one should attend to the sacred fires.
One should not neglect the five sacrifices by means of food grown without the plow.
And one should not abandon the private recitation of the Veda.
One should observe the practice of celibacy.
He should be clothed in leather or bark garments.
And he should wear his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails long.
One who lives like a pigeon may store up provisions for a month or for a year.
One who has accumulated [grain] for a year should discard what was previously accumulated on the full moon day of Āśvayuja.
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls brought from the village, using either a cupped leaf of the *palāśa* tree, his hand, or a wooden fragment.
The forest-dweller should wither his body through austerity.
In the summer, he should practice the penance of the five fires.
During the rainy season, he sleeps in the open air.
In the winter, one should wear wet clothes.
He should eat only at night.
One who subsists on flowers.
One who eats fruit.
One who eats vegetables.
Or he may subsist on leaves.
Or he may eat barley food once at each of the two ends of the fortnight.
Or he may subsist by means of Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
One who grinds with stones.
Or one who uses his teeth as a mortar.

This entire world of gods and humans has austerity as its root, austerity as its center, and austerity as its end; it is likewise sustained by austerity. Whatever is difficult to practice, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is distant, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—all that is achievable through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable.

Then, having ripened his inner impurities within the three stages of life, and having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice and given away all his possessions as the sacrificial fee, he should become one belonging to the stage of wandering mendicancy.
Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, he may enter the village for the purpose of begging alms.
He should practice alms-gathering from seven households.
One should not be distressed by failure to obtain [them].
One should not beg from a mendicant.
When the people have finished eating and have departed, he should collect alms when the vessels have been cleared away.
In a vessel made of clay, a wooden bowl, or a gourd vessel.
And their purification shall be by means of water.
One should be wary of gains obtained through being honored.
One should have an empty dwelling as one's abode.
Or one who makes the foot of a tree his dwelling.
He should not dwell for a second night in a village.
He should take only as much clothing as is necessary to cover his private parts; he should set down his foot purified by sight.
One should take water that has been filtered through a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth.
One should act in accordance with what is purified by the mind.
One should desire neither death nor life.
One should endure harsh words.
One should not despise anyone at all.
One should be free from desire.
Whether one person hews at his arm with an axe or another anoints the other with sandalwood paste, he should think neither ill of the former nor well of the latter.
One should be constant in breath control, concentration, and meditation.
One should perceive the impermanence of saṃsāra.
The impurity of the body.
Through old age, there is the transformation of form.
And [it experiences] affliction through bodily, mental, and adventitious diseases.
And with those that are innate.
Dwelling in the womb in perpetual darkness.
And in the midst of urine and excrement.
And therein, one experiences the sufferings of cold and heat.
At the time of birth, there is the experience of great suffering due to emerging from the narrowness of the womb.
In childhood, there is delusion and dependence upon the teacher.
From study comes manifold suffering.
And in youth, through the failure to obtain sense objects, or their acquisition by improper means, one falls into hell due to the indulgence in those objects.
Dwelling with those who are unpleasant and separation from those who are dear.
And there is very great suffering in hell, as well as in the migrations of saṃsāra and among the animal births.
Thus, in this ever-flowing cycle of existence, there is not the slightest bit of happiness.
Whatever is designated as "pleasure" in dependence upon the absence of suffering, that too is impermanent.
If one is unable to serve them, or if they are not obtained, there is great suffering.
And one should view this body as consisting of the seven constituent elements.
It consists of fat, blood, flesh, marrow, bone, pith, and semen.
Covered with skin.
And it is foul-smelling.
The seat of impurity.
Even when surrounded by hundreds of pleasures, it is subject to change.
Even if held with great effort, it is subject to destruction.
The locus of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy.
It consists of earth, water, fire, air, and space.
It is composed of bones, veins, arteries, and sinews.
A woman in her menses.
The sixfold skin.
It is supported by three hundred and sixty bones.
Their classification is as follows.
Including the minute teeth, there are sixty-four teeth in total.
There are twenty nails.
And the webbing between the fingers and toes.
There are sixty joints of the fingers.
Two on the two heels.
Four [finger-breadths] between the two elbows.
There are four [bones] in the two shanks.
Two each on the knees and the cheeks.
On the two shoulders.
On the palate, the uvula, and the pelvic bone.
The backbone consists of forty-five parts.
The neck consists of fifteen bones.
One [bone] in the collarbone.
Likewise, the jaw.
And at its root are two [fingers].
The two [parts] are the forehead, the eye, and the cheek.
The nose consists of solid bone.
Together with the arbudas and sthālakas, there are seventy-two side-protuberances.
The chest has seventeen [ribs].
There are two conch-like bones.
And there are four skull-fragments of the head.
In this body, there are seven hundred vessels.
There are nine hundred sinews.
There are two hundred vessels.
Five hundred muscles.
There are twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred and fifty-six minor vessels (dhamanīs).
There are three hundred thousand pores for the beard and hair.
There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas).
Two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores and sixty-seven lakhs of pores.
The navel, the anus, semen, blood, the two temples, the head, the throat, and the heart are the seats of the vital breaths.
The two arms, the two shanks, the waist, and the head are the six limbs.

Fat, the omentum, the place of its removal, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the kidneys, the bladder, the receptacle of feces, the stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the rectum, the abdomen, the pelvic cavity, the pupils, the eye-sockets,

the auditory canals, the ears, the ear-flaps, the cheeks, the eyebrows, the temples, the gums, the lips, the groins, the inguinal regions, the testicles, the testes, the kidneys, the two masses of phlegm, the breasts, the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, the shanks, the thighs, the calves, the sole of the foot, the belly, the top of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, and the nape of the neck— [all these are] in this [body].
And the objects of the senses are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
The nose, eyes, skin, tongue, and ear are the faculties of cognition (buddhīndriyas).
The hands, feet, anus, genitals, and tongue are the organs of action.
The mind, the intellect, the self, and the unmanifest—these are beyond the senses.
"O Earth, this body is designated as the 'field' (kṣetra); those who know this call him who understands it the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña)."
Know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O lady of noble nature; the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field must be constantly understood by one who seeks liberation.

With his feet placed extended upon his thighs, having laid his right hand upon his left, with his tongue motionless against the palate, not touching his teeth with his teeth, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the quarters, fearless and with a tranquil mind, he should contemplate that which transcends the twenty-four principles.
It is eternal, beyond the reach of the senses, devoid of qualities, transcending sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, omniscient, and exceedingly vast.
All-pervading and extremely subtle.
Having hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and possessing the power of all the senses everywhere.
One should meditate in this manner.
And for one devoted to meditation, the manifestation of yoga occurs within a year.

Then, having meditated upon each preceding one among earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, self, the unmanifest, and the puruṣa, and having attained proficiency therein, one should abandon that and meditate upon the next following one.
In this manner, one should begin the meditation on the person.
If one is still unable even for that, one should meditate on the Person like a lamp in the center of one's own heart-lotus, which is turned downwards.

If one is unable even for that, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—wearing a crown, earrings, and armlets; marked with the Śrīvatsa; his chest adorned with a forest garland; of gentle form; four-armed; bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; with the earth situated between his feet.
Whatever one meditates upon, that one attains; such is the secret of meditation.
Therefore, having abandoned everything that is perishable, one should meditate upon the imperishable alone.
And there is not even a single syllable that exists apart from the Puruṣa.
Having attained that, one becomes liberated.
Because the Great Lord, having pervaded the entire city [of the body], rests therein, he is therefore called "Puruṣa" by those who contemplate reality.
One should meditate upon the Puruṣa Viṣṇu, who is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa) and the twenty-fifth principle.
It is the self of reality, yet inaccessible; it is devoid of all principles, incapable [of action], yet the sustainer of all; it is without qualities, yet the enjoyer of qualities.
It exists both outside and within all beings, both as the unmoving and as the moving;
because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
Undivided, yet existing as if divided among all beings;

having the nature of the past, the future, and the present; it is the devourer and the progenitor. It is said to be the light even of lights, beyond darkness; it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge, seated in the heart of every being.
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been briefly described.
My devotee, having realized this, attains to my own state of being.
Having been addressed in this way, Vasumatī, having prostrated with her knees and head, spoke.
O Blessed One, in your presence these four elements have always made their abode: space in the form of a conch, wind in the form of a discus,
and fire in the form of a mace.
O you who have the form of a lotus! I too desire to move about at the feet of the Blessed One in this very same form.
Having been addressed in this way, the Blessed One said, "So be it."
Vasudhā, having obtained her desire, acted accordingly.
And he praised the God of gods.
Oṃ, homage to you!
God of gods.
Vāsudeva.
Primordial God.
Kāmadeva.
O Kāmapāla!
O protector of the earth!
O Prajāpati!
O Mahāprajāpatī!
O Lord of Vital Energy!
O Lord of Speech!
O Lord of the World!
O Lord of Heaven!
O Lord of the Forest!
O Lord of the milk!
O Lord of the Earth!
O Lord of Waters!
O Lord of the Quarters!
O Great Lord!
O Lord of the Maruts!
O Lord of Lakṣmī!
O you whose form is Brahman.
Beloved by the brahmins.
O all-pervading one!
Inconceivable.
To be realized through wisdom.
O you who are invoked by many!
O you who are praised by many!
Devoted to Brahman.
Beloved by Brahmā.
Belonging to the Brahmakāyika [heaven].
O you who belong to the Great Body!
Belonging to the Mahārājas.
The Caturmahārājika [devas].
Radiant.
O Great Radiant One!
Seven.
O highly fortunate one!
Svara.
Tuṣita.
Mahātuṣita.
O Pratardana!
Parinirmita.
Untransformed.
O you who possess mastery!
Sacrifice.
The great sacrifice.
The yoga of sacrifice.
Accessible through sacrifice.
O you whose conclusion is the sacrifice!
O Ajita!
Vaikuṇṭha.
The shoreless.
Purāṇa.
Supporter of progeny.
O wearer of the variegated crest!
O receiver of the sacrificial portion!
O Lord of All!
O sustainer of the universe!
O you of pure renown!
The worship of Acyuta.
Ghṛtārcis (He Whose Radiance is Ghee).
O Padmanābha!
Holder of the lotus.
O bearer of the stream of lotuses!
O One-Horned One!
O Great Boar!
O Immovable One.
Ananta.
The Person.
O Great Being!
Kapila.
Teacher of the Sāṃkhya school.
Viṣvaksena.
Dharma.
Giver of Dharma.
Bestower of boons.
O Viṣṇu!
O Victorious One!
O patient one!
Kṛṣṇa!
O lotus-eyed one!
Nārāyaṇa.
The ultimate refuge.
The ultimate refuge of the world.
Homage, homage! Thus [it is said].
Having thus praised her with a serene mind, the goddess Earth, having attained her desire, then spoke face-to-face to the Goddess.

Having seen the Goddess Śrī, who had taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, blazing with ascetic power and possessing the beautiful hue of well-refined gold, the Earth-goddess, filled with joy, questioned her.
To you who eternally dwell in the abode of a full-blown red lotus, and whose complexion is equal to the center of a full-blown red lotus.
O you with eyes like blue lotuses, with the complexion of refined gold, clad in white garments, your limbs adorned with jewels;
O moon-faced one, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, of great majesty, the foremost in the world!
You alone are the primary sleep of the world, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, Virati, and Jayā;
you are Kānti, Prabhā, Kīrti, as well as Vibhūti, Sarasvatī, Vāk, and Pāvanī.
Svadhā, Titikṣā, Vasudhā, Pratiṣṭhā, Sthiti, Sudīkṣā, as well as Sunīti; Khyāti, Viśālā, Anasūyā, Svāhā, Medhā, and likewise Buddhi.

O dark-eyed one, just as this best of gods stands having pervaded the entire triple world, so too do you stand, O giver of boons; nevertheless, O magnificent one, I ask you about the abode of your power.
Having been addressed in this way, Lakṣmī, standing before the best of gods, then spoke to the Earth: "O you of golden hue, I am always stationed at the side of the god Madhusūdana."

O Sustainer of the World, listen: by his command, those who are wise declare that I am he whom I remember in my mind, endowed with Śrī; furthermore, hear where I always abide when I am called to mind.
Likewise, when there is a cloud with hanging rain-clouds, enriched with Indra’s bow and flashing with lightning;
Likewise, O Earth, [he gazes] upon pure gold and silver, upon jewels and stainless garments, upon rows of palaces as white as snow, and upon temples adorned with banners.

When cow dung has just been spread, when a lordly elephant is in rut, when a horse is exultant, when a bull is likewise filled with pride, and when a Brahmin is similarly engaged in his Vedic studies; [in these cases, one should not step upon them].
I am likewise situated upon the lion-throne, the *āmalaka* fruit, the *bilva* fruit, the parasol, the conch, and the lotus; in the blazing fire, the stainless sword, and the reflection in the mirror.
In full water-jars adorned with yak-tail whisks and palm-leaf fans;

likewise in milk, clarified butter, and fresh grass; in honey, curd, and the bodies of matrons; in the body of a maiden, and in the bodies of the gods, ascetics, and those who have offered oblations in sacrifice.

Whether in the sound of an arrow, or when one has emerged from battle, or while standing [in battle], or when dead and gone to dwell in heaven; whether in the resonance of the Vedas, or in the sound of a conch, or in the utterance of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, or in the sound of musical instruments—[in all these cases, he remains].
Likewise at a royal consecration, a wedding, a sacrifice, or when one has bathed one's head; among white flowers, on mountains, with delightful fruits, and by the best of rivers.

In lakes full of water, as well as in waters and on ground covered with grass, in a cluster of lotuses, in a forest, in a calf, in a joyful infant, in a virtuous man devoted to dharma, in one who follows right conduct, in one constant in the study of the scriptures, in one of modest appearance, as well as in one who is well-attired,
in one who is perfectly pure and self-controlled, free from impurity, who eats wholesome food, and who honors guests.

To one who is content with his own wife, devoted to dharma, intensely committed to righteousness, free from overeating, always adorned with flowers, whose body is fragrant, anointed with perfumes, and well-ornamented;
When truth prevails, when people are devoted to the welfare of living beings, when they are endowed with patience and free from anger;
when women are always well-adorned, faithful to their husbands, sweet-spoken, generous-handed, blessed with sons, careful in guarding household goods, and fond of making offerings.
I always abide among women whose dwellings are well-cleaned, who have conquered their senses, who are free from malice, who are not covetous,
who regard righteousness, and who are endowed with compassion, as well as in Madhusūdana.
And for even a mere moment, I have never existed apart from the Supreme Person.
This preeminent treatise on Dharma was spoken by the Lord himself; those twice-born who uphold it shall attain the highest destination in heaven.
This is purifying, auspicious, conducive to heaven, and indeed life-prolonging; it is knowledge that brings fame and increases wealth and good fortune.

It should be studied, retained, recited, and heard; it should always be made to be heard by those who possess faith, by men desiring prosperity. That man who, desiring prosperity, constantly recites this [text] at all times—
